entries.defect: The struct name index was keyed only by name, so same-named structs from different modules collided and lookups could return another module's struct.

findings.summary: The fallback lookup for a `GenericInstance` with empty type args now matches a struct by name only. It ignores `module_source`, so it can return another module's struct that has the same name.
findings.detail: The old fallback loop required both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. The new code calls `type_table.find_struct_by_name(&name)` with no module check. `TypeTable::struct_name_index` maps a name to one `TypeId`, and a later intern overwrites an earlier one. When two modules define a struct with the same plain name (for example a user `Container` and a stdlib or other local `Container`), substitution inside a generic method can rewrite a type to the other module's struct. That gives wrong field layouts and types in later passes. The mangled-name lookups also changed from returning the first match to returning the last one interned.

findings.summary: The shared `known_type_names_cache` is built only from the global per-module maps. It no longer includes type names a module imports under an alias (`use { Foo as Bar }`), so `is_known_type_name("Bar")` now returns false.
findings.detail: The removed `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` also added the keys of the per-module flat maps (`struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `newtypes`, `generic_newtype_defs`, …). `build_module_map` inserts aliased imports into those maps under their local alias name. The new global set holds only the original names from the `all_*` maps. In a module that writes `impl Trait for Vec<Bar>` or `impl<Bar> ...`, or calls `Bar::method` (call.rs:463), the resolver now treats the aliased type as an unknown name. In `resolve_module`, `collect_function_signatures` and `find_trait_method_for_type` it then registers the name as a fresh type parameter or a blanket impl. Impls and calls resolve wrongly or report spurious errors.

findings.summary: `replace_type` does not update the new `struct_name_index`, so the index goes out of sync with `types` after a type is rewritten in place.
findings.detail: `replace_type` (used by boxing lowering to rewrite `Ref(prim)` into `Struct(Box<T>)`) writes directly into `self.types` without going through `intern`. A struct installed this way is never added to `struct_name_index`. If a struct is ever replaced by another type, its stale entry stays in the index. Any later `find_struct_by_name` call misses the rewritten struct or returns a `TypeId` that is no longer a struct. The old linear scan over `types` always saw the current state.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that find_struct_by_name keys only by name and ignores module_source, so same-named structs from different modules collide, which is exactly the defect fixed.

findings.summary: The fallback lookup for a plain struct in `substitute_type` no longer checks `module_source`, so a generic instance with no type arguments can be resolved to a struct of the same name from a different module.
findings.detail: The old fallback matched both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. The new code calls `type_table.find_struct_by_name(&name)`, which returns the struct with that name that was interned last, from any module. `struct_name_index` keeps one entry per name and later inserts overwrite earlier ones. So if two modules each define a struct with the same name (for example a user `Container` and a stdlib or other-module `Container`), an empty-arg `GenericInstance` for one of them can be replaced by the other module's struct's TypeId. That gives a wrong type, wrong field layout or wrong method dispatch in the generated code.

findings.summary: The shared known-type-names set is built only from the original names in the all_* maps, so local import aliases (`use { Foo as Bar }`) are no longer recognised as known types.
findings.detail: Before, `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` also read the per-module flat maps (`struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `enum_cases`, `flags_cases`, `newtypes`, `generic_newtype_defs`). Those maps come from `build_module_map`, which inserts the import's local alias name. The new `global_known_type_names` reads only `all_*` (keyed by declared names), so in the importing module `is_known_type_name("Bar")` now returns false. Its callers then misbehave. `find_trait_method_for_type` treats `impl Trait for Bar` as a blanket impl over a type parameter. `build_declared_type_params` and `collect_function_signatures` treat `Bar` as an undeclared generic type parameter. `resolve_call` no longer treats `Bar::method(...)` as a type-qualified call. The result is wrong method resolution or bogus diagnostics for code that compiled before.

findings.summary: `struct_name_index` is not updated by `replace_type`, and on duplicate names the last interned struct wins, while the old linear scan returned the first.
findings.detail: `intern` overwrites the index entry whenever another `Struct` with the same name is interned (for example with a different `module_source` or `is_monomorphized`/`base_name`). The old scan returned the first one in table order, so the mangled-name lookups in monomorphize can now return a different TypeId than before. Also, `replace_type` rewrites `types[id]` (for example `Ref(prim)` to `Struct(Box<T>)`) without adding the new struct name to the index, so `find_struct_by_name` misses structs created that way. The scan over `types` used to find them.

grade.reason: Finding 0 says find_struct_by_name ignores module_source, so same-named structs from different modules collide in the name-only index, and the lookup can return the other module's struct. That is the known defect.

findings.summary: The fallback lookup for a `GenericInstance` with empty type args no longer checks `module_source`, so it can return a struct with the same name from a different module.
findings.detail: The old fallback matched on both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. The new code calls `type_table.find_struct_by_name(&name)`, which looks up a name-only index. When two modules define a struct with the same name (for example a user `Value` and `Value` in `core:json_value`, or `Point` in two local modules), the empty-args `GenericInstance` from one module's generic methods can be swapped for the other module's struct. That gives wrong field layouts or types, a miscompile or a confusing type error.

findings.summary: `struct_name_index` keeps only the most recently interned `TypeId` per name, so lookups now return the last matching struct where the old scans returned the first.
findings.detail: `intern` runs `struct_name_index.insert(name.clone(), id)` for every Struct, so a later Struct with the same name replaces the earlier entry. That later entry can come from another module, or be the same name with a different `is_monomorphized`/`base_name`. The removed loops walked `iter_type_ids()` in insertion order and returned the first match. The monomorphizer's mangled-name lookups can therefore resolve to a different `TypeId` than before when names collide. `retain` rebuilds the index the same last-wins way. `replace_type`, used by boxing to rewrite a slot into a `Box<T>` Struct, never updates the index, so later lookups by name can miss that struct.

findings.summary: The shared known-type-names set drops the local names a module gets from aliased imports (`use { Foo as Bar }`), so `is_known_type_name("Bar")` now returns false.
findings.detail: The removed `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` read each resolver's own maps (`struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `enum_cases`, `flags_cases`, `newtypes`, `generic_newtype_defs`). `build_module_map` adds the alias as a key in those maps. The new global set is built only from the original names in the `all_*` maps, so aliases are never in it. Code that relies on `is_known_type_name` (in method_lookup, e.g. telling `Bar::method()` or a type-name path apart from a value) now treats aliased imported types as unknown. Valid programs that use import aliases for types can then fail to resolve or be resolved differently.

grade.reason: Finding 0 points out that `find_struct_by_name(&name)` uses a name-only index and ignores module_source, so a same-named struct from another module can be returned, which is the known defect.

entries.defect: compile_one used a silent host and threw away the compiler's diagnostics, both through `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")` and by silently producing empty output when the dump returned None, so fixture-generation failures were reported with no reason.

findings.summary: Passing --skip-empty also hides real compile failures. Every phase run in update-golden-format-fixtures.sh passes it, so a broken format fixture now just loses its golden file and the script still succeeds.
findings.detail: In the writer, the `Err(e)` branch (compilation failed, WAT generation failed) is controlled by `skip_empty` in the same way as the empty-output branch. It deletes the existing output file, prints "Skipped", adds to skip_count, and moves on. The old script stopped with exit 1 on any failed or empty dump, and it skipped only `#![no_prelude]` files, found explicitly with grep. Now every phase command passes --skip-empty. If a regression stops `all.dirty.wado` or `mess.dirty.wado` from compiling, their .tir/.lower/.wir/.wat goldens are deleted, the final assert still holds because the skip is counted, and the script ends with "Golden format fixtures updated." A missed error becomes lost golden data.

findings.summary: If every dump worker panics (for example, a compiler panic that most fixtures trigger), the tool hangs forever instead of failing.
findings.detail: The main thread still holds `read_rx` (the `Arc<Mutex<Receiver>>`) during the whole write loop and the joins, so the read channel never closes from the receiver's side. When all workers die, each one drops its `write_tx` clone, the writer loop ends, and `reader.join()` is called. The reader thread, though, is blocked in `read_tx.send(item)` on the full bounded channel (capacity 2*num_workers) and nothing will ever receive. With more fixtures than workers + 2*workers, which is the normal case, the process deadlocks. The old code caught a worker's death per task ("compiler thread panicked") and stopped with an error.

findings.summary: When one worker panics, its fixture is dropped without being reported, and the fixtures that worker would have compiled leave no result. The run only fails at the final join, with no hint of which file caused it.
findings.detail: A panic in `compile_one` (a compiler bug) unwinds the worker thread. The panicking item never reaches the writer, and its old output file stays on disk unchanged. The run only fails at `w.join().expect("dump worker panicked")`, with no file name attached. The old implementation turned this into a per-file error naming the output path.

grade.reason: None of the findings mention that compiler diagnostics are discarded via map_err or that a None dump silently yields empty output; they cover --skip-empty hiding failures and how worker panics are handled.

findings.summary: Every golden-dump call now passes `--skip-empty`, so a format fixture that fails to compile is skipped without an error and its existing golden file is deleted.
findings.detail: In `run_pipeline`, when `skip_empty` is set the `Err(e)` branch calls `fs::remove_file(&item.output_path)`, prints "Skipped", counts the file as skipped and carries on. The script only meant this flag to cover no_prelude files. In practice it hides every compiler regression or failure on the dirty fixtures: the .tir, .lower, .optimize, .wir and .wat goldens for that fixture are deleted and the script still exits 0. The old `run_dump` kept the existing target and ran `exit 1` with a warning on any failure or empty output. The final `success + skip == total` assertion does not catch this either, because these failures are counted as skips.

findings.summary: Generation now runs one compiler thread per CPU, dropping the half-CPU cap the old bulk mode used to stop crashes and memory exhaustion.
findings.detail: The removed `run_bulk` capped concurrent compiler threads at `available_parallelism()/2` (minimum 2). Its comments say this keeps peak memory bounded and avoids SIGSEGV under memory pressure, since each compilation uses a 16 MB stack plus a large heap. `run_pipeline` starts `num_workers = available_parallelism()` workers, each with a 16 MB stack and a leaked 8 MB alternate signal stack, and runs compilations fully in parallel. This brings back the out-of-memory and SIGSEGV failures the cap was added to prevent when `update-golden-fixtures` runs over the whole fixture directory on machines with many cores.

findings.summary: The `.tir.wado` goldens now hold only the optimized entry-point module, so they lose the other modules the old `dump --tir` output had and become byte-identical to `.optimize.wado`.
findings.detail: In `compile_one`, `Phase::Tir` prints only the entry-point module of `optimized_project`. The old `wado dump --tir` printed every module, including core:allocator, core:builtin and String. The regenerated `all.tir.wado`, `mess.tir.wado` and the others drop all non-entry modules, so changes in those modules no longer show up in the goldens.

findings.summary: The WIR and TIR golden headers always say "with -O2 optimization", whatever `-O` level was requested.
findings.detail: `compile_one` writes the fixed text "// Golden file: WIR with -O2 optimization" or "Optimized TIR with -O2 optimization" even when `opt_level` is O0, O1, O3 or Os. Goldens generated at another level therefore describe themselves wrongly.

grade.reason: No finding notes that compile_one throws away the silent host's diagnostics via `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")` or quietly emits empty output when the dump returns None; finding 0 is about `--skip-empty` hiding and deleting failed fixtures, which is a different cause.

findings.summary: With `--skip-empty`, a format fixture that fails to compile is now skipped quietly: its golden file is deleted and the script still exits successfully.
findings.detail: In `pipeline.rs`, the `Err(e)` branch checks `skip_empty` just like the empty-output branch does. It logs 'Skipped ...', removes the output file and continues. The script passes `--skip-empty` on every golden-dump call so that the `no_prelude` fixture is tolerated. So if a compiler regression breaks `all`, `mess` or `ops.*`, their .tir/.lower/.optimize/.wir/.wat files are deleted and the script prints 'Golden format fixtures updated.' The old `run_dump` exited with status 1 when a command failed or produced empty output.

findings.summary: Compile errors are no longer printed: `compile_one` uses a silent host and reports only 'compilation failed'.
findings.detail: The removed `run_bulk` built `FilesystemCompilerHost::new`, which prints diagnostics at Info level, so a fixture that failed under `update-golden-fixtures` showed the real compiler error. The new code uses `FilesystemCompilerHost::silent`, and `compile_with_options` gets `log_level: Off`. The collected diagnostics are never read. When a golden fixture breaks, the panic says only 'compilation failed', with no location or message.

findings.summary: The worker count was raised from half the CPUs to all of them, which brings back the memory-pressure crashes the old cap guarded against.
findings.detail: The old `run_bulk` capped parallelism at `available_parallelism()/2`, with a comment saying this bounded peak memory and avoided SIGSEGV under memory pressure. Each compiler thread has a 16 MB stack, an 8 MB alternate signal stack and a large heap. `run_pipeline` now starts `available_parallelism()` workers, each running a full O2 compilation at once. That roughly doubles peak memory, so a crash or OOM kill partway through regeneration of the full fixtures set is more likely.

findings.summary: The regenerated `.tir.wado` golden files lost content: they hold only the optimized entry module, so they are identical to `.optimize.wado` and no longer show the other modules.
findings.detail: `--phase tir` takes the `Phase::Tir` path, which writes only the module where `is_entry_point()` is true and labels it 'Optimized TIR with -O2 optimization'. The old `wado dump --tir` wrote every module (allocator, builtin, prelude, wasi:cli and so on), as the deleted lines in the diff show. The format-fixture TIR output for library modules is no longer captured, so changes there no longer show up in these golden files.

grade.reason: Finding 1 identifies that compile_one uses a silent host and discards the collected diagnostics, so failures report only 'compilation failed'. That is the root cause the fix addresses.

entries.defect: The .tagpr config put keys outside a [tagpr] section, where tagpr silently ignores them, and used `command` (which runs before the version bump) instead of `postVersionCommand`, so Cargo.lock was never synced and `cargo --locked` CI broke.

findings.summary: The .tagpr file has no `[tagpr]` section header, so it is not valid git-config and tagpr cannot read its settings; `release = patch` is also not a value tagpr accepts.
findings.detail: tagpr reads its config with `git config -f .tagpr tagpr.<key>`, so every key must sit under a `[tagpr]` section. Here `versionFile`, `command` and `release` come before any section header. git rejects this as a bad config line, so tagpr either fails outright or ignores the settings. If they are ignored, Cargo.toml is not bumped and `cargo update --workspace` never runs. Separately, `tagpr.release` controls whether a GitHub Release is created (true/false/draft); it is not the default bump kind, so `patch` is either invalid or misread. The default bump is already patch.

findings.summary: The tagpr step never gets a GITHUB_TOKEN, so tagpr cannot open the release PR or push the tag.
findings.detail: Songmu/tagpr reads the token from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable; the documented usage sets `env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`. The workflow grants `contents`/`pull-requests: write` but never exposes the token to the step. tagpr will fail on every push to main, so no release PR or tag is ever created.

findings.summary: release.yml relies on the tag push that tagpr makes, but a tag pushed with the default GITHUB_TOKEN does not start other workflows.
findings.detail: GitHub does not start workflows from events created with the repository GITHUB_TOKEN, to prevent recursive runs. Even once tagpr has a token, a `v*` tag it pushes with GITHUB_TOKEN will not trigger `on: push: tags: v*`. The automated path described in .tagpr (merge the release PR, tag is pushed, release.yml publishes) therefore never produces a release. It needs a PAT or GitHub App token, or tagpr's `tag` output used to call the release job from tagpr.yml.

grade.reason: Finding 0 points out that versionFile, command and release sit outside the [tagpr] section, so tagpr ignores them and `cargo update` never syncs Cargo.lock, which is the core of the known defect (it does not mention the `command` vs `postVersionCommand` timing issue).

findings.summary: The keys in .tagpr sit outside a `[tagpr]` section, so tagpr cannot read its config: either the file fails to parse or versionFile and command are ignored.
findings.detail: tagpr reads .tagpr as a git-config file and looks up keys like `tagpr.versionFile`, `tagpr.command` and `tagpr.release`. This file has no `[tagpr]` header, and git config rejects a key with no section. So either the tagpr job fails on every push to main, or the settings never apply. Then Cargo.toml is not bumped and `cargo update --workspace` never runs, so the Release PR's version won't match its tag and the `bump-version --check` step in release.yml fails.

findings.summary: `release = patch` does not set the default bump kind; `tagpr.release` decides whether tagpr creates a GitHub Release (true/false/draft).
findings.detail: Even under a proper `[tagpr]` section, `tagpr.release = patch` is not a valid value for that setting. tagpr either rejects it or treats it as an unexpected boolean. The intended effect, a default patch bump, doesn't need this key at all. tagpr's own GitHub Release creation could also clash with the release created by release.yml's softprops/action-gh-release step.

findings.summary: The tag tagpr pushes with the default GITHUB_TOKEN will not trigger release.yml, so no release is built automatically.
findings.detail: tagpr.yml runs Songmu/tagpr with the default GITHUB_TOKEN, and GitHub does not start new workflow runs for refs pushed with that token. When the Release PR is merged, tagpr pushes `vX.Y.Z`, but the `on: push: tags: 'v*'` trigger in release.yml never fires. Step 4 of the documented flow ('release.yml runs on the tag push') never happens; each release needs a manual workflow_dispatch, or a PAT/GitHub App token passed to tagpr.

findings.summary: The `.tagpr` file has no `[tagpr]` section header, so tagpr cannot read it and the release automation fails.
findings.detail: tagpr reads `.tagpr` with git-config, which needs every key inside a section such as `[tagpr]`, with keys like `versionFile`, `command` and `vPrefix` under it. Here the keys sit at the top of the file with no section. git-config rejects that ("key does not contain a section") or tagpr ignores the keys. Either way tagpr.yml fails on every push to main, or it runs without `versionFile` and `command`, so the release PR never updates the Cargo.toml version and Cargo.lock as intended.

findings.summary: tagpr pushes the release tag with the default GITHUB_TOKEN, and GitHub does not start other workflows from such pushes, so release.yml never runs on the tag.
findings.detail: release.yml is triggered by `push: tags: v*`. GitHub does not start workflow runs for events made with the repository GITHUB_TOKEN, so the tag tagpr creates after the Release PR merges starts no release build. No binaries are published unless someone runs workflow_dispatch by hand. The step also passes no `GITHUB_TOKEN` env, which tagpr's documented setup expects; without it the action may not authenticate at all. The fix is a PAT or GitHub App token, or having tagpr.yml call release.yml directly.

findings.summary: `release = patch` is not a bump-kind setting in tagpr; `release` controls whether tagpr creates a GitHub Release.
findings.detail: In tagpr, `tagpr.release` takes true, false or draft and decides whether and how tagpr creates the GitHub Release. Setting it to `patch` is invalid or treated as an unexpected value. The bump kind does not come from here: patch is already the default and labels override it. So this line does not do what its comment says, and it may make tagpr's Release creation fail or behave unexpectedly alongside the release created by release.yml.

entries.defect: The response body pump awaited `frame_tx.send` with no time bound, so a client that stopped draining but kept its connection open pinned the handler task's fiber stack forever.

findings.summary: The epoch deadline is refreshed only when the dispatch loop turns. A worker that gets no new jobs and finishes no requests for longer than `timeout+5`s traps the moment wasm runs again, and every request on that store is lost.
findings.detail: `set_epoch_deadline(epoch_ticks)` sets the deadline to the current epoch plus `timeout+5` ticks. It is renewed only after a `Step` is produced, which needs a new job or a finished in-flight request. A request can legitimately wait on the host for a long time: streaming a large body to a slow client blocked on `frame_tx.send`, an outbound HTTP call, or a long sleep. If no other traffic reaches that worker meanwhile, the deadline passes while no wasm is running. The next time the guest resumes it hits the deadline and traps, because the engine is configured with the default trap behaviour. `run_concurrent` returns `Err`, and the worker drops every in-flight request on that store and rebuilds. So healthy long-running requests on a quiet server are killed. The old code reset the deadline per request on a fresh store, so this did not happen.

findings.summary: A request stuck on a host await is never timed out, and it can stall its worker for good during a recycle drain. New requests sent to that worker then hang with no 504.
findings.detail: The wall-clock `tokio::time::timeout` around `run_concurrent` was removed, and the epoch deadline cannot preempt a host await. A client that stops reading a streamed body leaves its `HandlerTask` pending forever. Once `handled >= recycle_requests`, the worker stops calling `job_rx.recv()` and waits for `inflight` to drain, which never happens. `Dispatch::submit` keeps sending to that worker in round-robin order. When its bounded channel is full, `submit(...).await` blocks, and that await happens before the first-byte timeout is armed in `dispatch_request`. A single slow or malicious client can therefore wedge 1/N of the server's request capacity until the process restarts.

findings.summary: `max_concurrency` does not limit in-flight requests: each worker spawns every job it receives with no cap, so the fixed fiber-stack pool can run out.
findings.detail: `chan_cap = max_concurrency / workers` only limits jobs still queued in the channel. The worker loop keeps receiving jobs and pushing `accessor.spawn(HandlerTask…)` into `inflight` with no upper bound. Each spawned guest task needs an async fiber stack from the pool, and `pool.total_stacks(max_concurrency)` sizes that pool as if in-flight work were capped. Under load, or with slow handlers, the number of live tasks exceeds `total_stacks`. Stack allocation then fails, which errors the store (all in-flight requests are lost and the worker rebuilds) or fails the requests. That defeats the documented purpose of `--max-concurrency`.

findings.summary: One trapping request now poisons a shared instance, which breaks every other request on that worker until it is recycled.
findings.detail: All requests on a worker now run as tasks on one long-lived component instance. If a single handler traps, for example on a guest panic or `unreachable`, `HandlerTask` catches the `service.handle(...)` error and returns `Ok(())`, so `run_concurrent` does not fail and the worker does not rebuild. Wasmtime marks a component instance that has trapped as not re-enterable, so the remaining concurrent requests and up to `recycle_requests` (default 10000) later requests on that worker fail with 500s. Before this change each request had its own fresh store and instance, so a trap affected only that request.

grade.reason: Finding 2 identifies that a client which stops reading a streamed body leaves the HandlerTask pending forever with no timeout on the host await, which is the unbounded frame_tx.send pump defect.

findings.summary: `dispatch_request` waits on `Dispatch::submit` before starting the first-byte timeout, so when a worker stops reading its queue (draining for a recycle, or wedged), every request routed to that worker hangs with no timeout and no 504.
findings.detail: `submit` calls `mpsc::Sender::send(job).await`, which blocks while the worker's bounded queue (`max_concurrency / workers` slots) is full. The `tokio::time::sleep(timeout)` race only starts after `submit` returns. Once a worker reaches `recycle_requests`, `worker_loop` stops calling `job_rx.recv()` until every in-flight task has finished. The old per-request wall-clock `tokio::time::timeout` around `run_concurrent` was removed, so nothing bounds an in-flight task that is stuck on a host await (for example a client that keeps the connection open but never reads the body, which blocks `frame_tx.send`) or that awaits something that never resolves. When that happens the recycle never finishes, the queue fills, and every Nth request (round-robin) blocks in `submit` forever. The worker also never handles another request.

findings.summary: Nothing ends a stuck request any more, so a stuck task and its store resources are kept for the life of the worker.
findings.detail: Before this change each request's store was dropped after `timeout` because `tokio::time::timeout` wrapped `run_concurrent`. Now `HandlerTask`s run inside a long-lived `run_concurrent`, and the only bound left is the epoch deadline, which only fires while wasm is executing. A handler waiting on a host future (a slow body consumer, a never-completing guest future or stream) is never cancelled. It holds its fiber stack, resources and memory until the instance is recycled, and with `--recycle-requests 0` that is never. These piling up use up the pool and cause the worker stall described above.

findings.summary: Nothing caps the number of in-flight requests per worker, so the pooling allocator's stack pool (`total_stacks = max_concurrency`) can run out under load.
findings.detail: The comment on `chan_cap` says the per-worker queues keep in-flight work at or below `max_concurrency`. But `worker_loop` takes jobs off the channel straight away and pushes them into `inflight` with no limit. The channel capacity only bounds jobs that are queued, not jobs that are running. Each concurrent guest task needs an async fiber stack from the pool, and instantiations in other workers draw on the same pool. With enough slow concurrent requests, stack allocation fails, which surfaces as handler errors or traps on the worker's store instead of back-pressure.

findings.summary: All requests now share one store and instance per worker, so a single trapping request (for example a Wado `panic`) can break every other request on that worker.
findings.detail: Previously every request had its own store, so a trap only affected that request. Now a trap in one `HandlerTask` happens in the shared component instance. This likely leaves the instance poisoned: after a trap the Component Model does not let the instance be entered again, and later requests fail with 500 until the next recycle, which could be up to 10000 requests away. Or the trap ends `run_concurrent` with `Err`, which drops every concurrent in-flight request on that worker; the code itself says 'In-flight requests on the trapped store are lost'. The same thing happens when a request waits on host I/O for more than `timeout+5`s while the loop is idle: when the guest resumes, the epoch deadline has passed and the whole instance traps. In each case, malformed input to one request can disrupt unrelated clients.

grade.reason: Finding 0 states that nothing bounds an in-flight task blocked on `frame_tx.send` when a client keeps the connection open but never reads the body, which leaves the task stuck forever; this is the same unbounded body-pump send the fix addresses.

findings.summary: A recycle waits with no time limit for in-flight requests to finish, so one stuck request can freeze a worker for good.
findings.detail: When `handled >= recycle_requests`, `worker_loop` stops reading `job_rx` and loops on `inflight.next()` until every spawned `HandlerTask` ends. The PR removed the old `tokio::time::timeout` around request handling, and the first-byte 504 in `dispatch_request` does not cancel the guest task. A task can therefore stay in flight forever: a client that stops reading the body leaves `frame_tx.send().await` blocked, and a guest can await something that never resolves. In either case the worker never finishes its recycle and never takes another job. Its queue fills, and requests routed to it hang.

findings.summary: `dispatch.submit(job).await` runs before the timeout race starts, so requests to a stalled worker hang with no 504.
findings.detail: `Dispatch::submit` assigns requests to workers round-robin and awaits `send` on a bounded per-worker channel. The 30s first-byte `sleep` is only raced after that send succeeds. If a worker's queue is full because the worker is stuck draining a recycle, blocked by a runaway guest, or rebuilding after a trap, `submit` blocks with no limit. Round-robin keeps sending 1/N of all traffic to that worker even when the others are idle, so those clients get neither a response nor a timeout.

findings.summary: The epoch deadline is only renewed when the dispatch loop turns, so a long but healthy request traps and takes down the whole worker.
findings.detail: `set_epoch_deadline(epoch_ticks)` is refreshed only after the dispatch loop wakes. If one request spends more than timeout+5 seconds waiting on the host while no other job arrives, the deadline passes during that wait. Examples are streaming a large body to a slow reader or awaiting a slow outbound call. The guest's next wasm instruction then raises an epoch interrupt trap. `run_concurrent` returns `Err`, the store is dropped, and that request plus every other in-flight request on the worker is aborted. The new docs say the timeout only covers time to the first byte, yet a request can still be killed after its head was sent.

findings.summary: Any guest trap now aborts every concurrent request on the same worker, not just the request that trapped.
findings.detail: All requests on a worker run as `Accessor::spawn` tasks in one store. A guest trap, such as a Wado `panic` or a failed `unwrap` compiled to `unreachable`, poisons that store, so `run_concurrent` fails for all of them. The other in-flight requests lose their `resp_tx` and get a 500 "Handler aborted", or have their streamed bodies cut off. Before this change each request had its own store, so a failure stayed with the request that caused it.

findings.summary: The number of in-flight requests is not actually capped by `max_concurrency`, so the fixed fiber-stack pool can run out under load.
findings.detail: The comments claim the queues bound in-flight work to `max_concurrency / workers` per worker, matching `pool.total_stacks(max_concurrency)`. In fact the dispatch loop keeps taking jobs from `job_rx` while others are in flight and pushes each into an unbounded `FuturesUnordered`. The channel capacity only limits jobs that are queued, not jobs that are running. Each worker store also needs its own stack for instantiation and `run_concurrent`. With enough slow concurrent requests, the guest tasks plus the workers' own stacks exceed the pool, fiber allocation fails, the store errors, and all in-flight requests on that worker are lost.

grade.reason: Finding 0 names the same root cause: a client that stops reading the body leaves the unbounded `frame_tx.send().await` blocked, so the handler task stays in flight forever. It frames the harm as a frozen recycle rather than a pinned fiber stack, but it is the same code and the same missing time bound.

entries.defect: The dataflow walker treated labeled blocks as straight-line code. It recorded no state at a labeled `break`, so the post-block state ignored early-exit paths that skipped syncs emitted inside the block. Later code then missed a re-read or write-back, and the field update was lost (the indent_level drift).

findings.summary: A labeled `break` that leaves the HFS loop no longer writes the scalar back to the field, and the post-loop write-back was removed, so updates to the field are lost.
findings.detail: In `walk_stmt`, the `Break { label: Some(_) }` arm never calls `commit_scalar_for_escape`. The old code wrote back before any break whose label did not enclose it, and `scalarize_loop` now returns an empty `post_stmts`. This shows up when the HFS loop sits inside a labeled block, which is common after inlining: a function containing a loop is inlined, so its `return` becomes `break __inline_xxx: v` and jumps out of the loop. If the scalar is in the `ScalarOnly` state at that point, the latest value of `obj.field` stays in `__hfs_F` and never reaches the struct. Code after the loop then reads a stale field.

findings.summary: Sync statements produced while walking a sub-expression are all placed before the whole statement, so a re-read needed after a call runs before that call.
findings.detail: `walk_expr` pushes `make_re_read_stmt` into `out`, the list of statements emitted before the enclosing statement. The same happens for write-backs from `walk_call_expr`. Take `let a = f(&mut b) + b.v;` or `if !(f(&mut b) > b.v) { break; }`. Walking `f(&mut b)` sets the state to `FieldOnly`, and the read of `b.v` that follows emits `__hfs_v = b.v` into `out`. That re-read executes before `f` is called. The rewritten `__hfs_v` read after the call therefore returns the value from before the call and misses `f`'s change. `b.v = f(&mut b) + b.v` goes wrong in the same way. Only Block, If, Match and Switch sub-bodies get their own statement lists. Binary operators, call arguments and the like do not.

findings.summary: The state after a nested loop is JOIN(entry, state at body end), which can say `ScalarOnly` when the loop actually exited at a `break` while the field held the latest value, so later reads use a stale scalar.
findings.detail: Take `loop { call(&mut x); if c { break; } x.f = 1; }` inside the HFS loop. At the break the state is `FieldOnly`: the call changed the field, and `commit_scalar_for_escape` does nothing for `FieldOnly`. The walk reaches the end of the body in `ScalarOnly`, and `pick_join_target_for_candidate(Both, ScalarOnly)` gives `ScalarOnly`. After the inner loop the walker therefore emits no re-read before reading `__hfs_f`, but at runtime the scalar is stale and the field holds the call's result. The old code re-read after every call, so this case was safe.

findings.summary: A labeled block is walked as straight-line code, so the state recorded after the block ignores early `break label` exits, and a later re-read can overwrite a scalar value that was never written back.
findings.detail: In `walk_stmt`, the `LabeledBlock` arm (and `walk_inline_block`) only continues with the state at the block's fall-through end. Example: `l: { x.f = v; if c { break l; } g(&mut x); }`. On the break path the scalar holds the latest value and the field is stale (`ScalarOnly`). After the block the walker believes `FieldOnly`, because of `g`, so the next read of `x.f` emits `__hfs_f = x.f`. When the break was taken, that statement replaces the new scalar value with the stale field and the write of `v` is lost. The removed `inline_block_written` guard used to keep these candidates from being scalarized at all, which covered the inliner's `__inline_*` blocks.

grade.reason: Finding 3 describes the same defect: labeled blocks are walked as straight-line code, so the post-block state ignores `break label` exits, and later sync decisions (re-reads or write-backs) are wrong and lose the field update.

findings.summary: A labeled `break` that leaves the HFS loop never writes the scalar back to the field, and there is no post-loop write-back any more, so the scalar's latest value is lost.
findings.detail: `walk_stmt` calls `commit_scalar_for_escape` only for an unlabeled `Break`. A `break <label>` is left alone even when its label does not enclose the current position. The old `enclosing_labels` check, which caught that case, was removed, and `post_stmts` is now always empty. The inliner turns each `return` of an inlined body into `break __inline_X: v` (inline.rs:2115-2121). So when an inlined function contains the HFS loop and that loop has an early `return`, the break leaves the loop while the candidate is `ScalarOnly`. The write to `obj.field` is then dropped, and callers see a stale field value. The same happens for any break to a labeled block that wraps the loop.

findings.summary: Labeled blocks inside the loop ignore the state at their `break` points, so the code after the block (including the body-end sync) can clobber a scalar write or read a stale scalar.
findings.detail: For `LabeledBlock`, the walker runs `walk_block` and treats the fall-through state as the state after the block. It does not join in the states at `break label`. Example: `lbl: { x.v = 1; if c { break lbl; } f(&mut x); }`. On the break path the candidate is `ScalarOnly` (the field is stale). On the fall-through path it is `FieldOnly`. The body-end sync drives `FieldOnly` to `Both` with a re-read `__hfs = x.v`. When the break is taken, that re-read overwrites the scalar 1 with the old field value, so the write is lost. In the reverse case (a `&mut` call right before the break, then a scalar write on fall-through), later reads use a stale scalar.

findings.summary: After a nested loop, the outer state is computed from the inner body's linear exit state, not from its `break` points, so the code after the loop can read a stale scalar.
findings.detail: `walk_nested_loop` sets the post-loop state to JOIN(entry, body_exit_pre_sync). Consider an inner body like `if cond { bump(&mut s); break; } s.pos = s.pos + 1;`. On the break path the candidate is `FieldOnly`, and the convergence sync for the then-block is appended after the `break`, where it never runs. The linear walk ends at `ScalarOnly`, so the join gives `ScalarOnly`. A later outer read of `s.pos` then emits no re-read and uses the stale `__hfs_pos` instead of the value `bump` wrote. The unlabeled-break commit only handles `ScalarOnly` candidates, not `FieldOnly` ones.

findings.summary: A re-read needed for a field read that follows a `&mut` call in the same expression is placed before the whole statement, so it runs before the call and the read sees a stale value.
findings.detail: `walk_call_expr` sets the candidate to `FieldOnly` after the call. A later read in the same expression then pushes `make_re_read_stmt` into `out`, but `out` holds statements that are emitted before the enclosing statement. For `if p.advance() && p.pos < n` or `sum = f(&mut b) + b.v`, the re-read runs before `advance`/`f`, and the rewritten `__hfs_pos` read after the call returns the value from before the call. The new design claims to track these transitions precisely, but here it produces a wrong result.

grade.reason: Finding 1 matches the known defect: the walker treats labeled blocks as straight-line code and never joins in the states at `break label`, so code after the block makes the wrong re-read or write-back decision and the field update is lost.

findings.summary: A labeled `break` that leaves the HFS loop never writes the scalar back to the field, and the post-loop write-back was removed, so scalar-only updates are lost.
findings.detail: `walk_stmt` calls `commit_scalar_for_escape` only for unlabeled `break` (`if label.is_none()`). `scalarize_loop` now returns an empty `post_stmts`, on the claim that every exit path already commits. That claim is false for labeled breaks. Desugaring rewrites every unlabeled `break` inside a C-style `for` into `break __for_N`, which targets a labeled block outside the `Loop`. User-labeled breaks to outer blocks behave the same way. So `for ... { self.x = v; if c { break; } }` reaches `break __for_N` with `__hfs_x` holding the value, the field never receives it, and code after the loop reads the stale field. The old code wrote back before any break whose label did not enclose it, and also had the post-loop write-back.

findings.summary: After a labeled block, the state comes only from the fall-through path. A `break label` taken with a different state (such as an inlined `return`) leaves the scalar or the field stale.
findings.detail: The `LabeledBlock` arm just calls `walk_block(inner, states, ctx)` and keeps the end-of-block state; break-target states are not tracked. Two places hit this. One is inlined `&mut self` methods, where `return` becomes `break __inline_*`. The other is `continue` inside a `for`, which becomes `break __for_N_body`. Example: `blk: { __hfs = v /*ScalarOnly*/; if c { break blk; } helper(&mut self) /*FieldOnly*/ }`. After the block the walker believes FieldOnly, so the next read re-reads the field, but on the break path the field was never written and the scalar update is lost. The reverse case (FieldOnly on the break path, Both at the block end) reads a stale scalar. This PR also removed the `collect_locals_accessed_inside_inline_blocks` guard, which used to keep such locals from being scalarized, so these inlined-method shapes are now exposed.

findings.summary: `walk_nested_loop` sets the state after the loop to JOIN(entry, body_exit) and ignores the state at the inner loop's `break`, so the outer code can read a stale scalar.
findings.detail: An inner (non-HFS) `Loop` can only exit through `break`/`return`. The state at the break point can be FieldOnly even when the body's linear end state is Both. Example inner body: `bump(&mut s); if done { break; } let t = s.pos /*re-read -> Both*/;`. Here entry=Both and body_exit=Both, so the walker assumes Both after the loop and adds no re-read. At runtime the break leaves `s.pos` updated by `bump` while `__hfs_pos` holds the old value, so an outer read of `s.pos` after the inner loop gets the wrong value. Unlabeled `break` only commits ScalarOnly, so FieldOnly at the break is never re-read.

findings.summary: When a scalarized field is read after a `&mut` call in the same statement, the re-read is emitted before the whole statement, so the read sees the value from before the call.
findings.detail: `walk_call_expr` sets the state to FieldOnly, and a later `field_read_to_candidate` in the same expression then pushes `make_re_read_stmt` into `out`. `out` holds statements inserted before the enclosing statement, not at the read's position in the expression. For `sum = f(&mut b) + b.v;` (or `let x = f(&mut b) + b.v`, or `g(&mut b) > 0 && b.v > 3`), the re-read runs before `f`, and `b.v` is rewritten to `__hfs_v`. The read therefore returns the value from before the call, not the field as `f` mutated it. The state is then marked Both even though the field has changed, so later reads in the iteration are also stale.

grade.reason: Finding 1 matches the known defect: the LabeledBlock arm takes only the fall-through state, so labeled-break exit states are never joined in and the scalar or field is left stale after the block.

entries.defect: can_move_past only checked whether the intervening statement clobbers the moved expression's reads, not the reverse; a call-containing field initializer could therefore be relocated past an intervening read of a global it mutates, a miscompile.

findings.summary: `can_move_past` checks only one direction: whether the skipped statement clobbers what the moved initializer reads. It never checks whether the initializer's own writes or calls affect what the skipped statement reads or writes, so side effects can be reordered.
findings.detail: The relaxed pass no longer requires the field initializer to be re-evaluation safe, so `inner` can contain a `Call`, a `GlobalSet`, a `LocalTee` or a heap/memory store. `can_move_past` returns `!int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)`, which only asks whether the intervening statement's writes overlap the initializer's reads. Take `self = struct.new Box{ value: bump_counter() }; x = global.get COUNTER; use(self.value)`. The intervening `x = COUNTER` is Linear, cannot trap and writes nothing, so it is skipped. The call then moves after the read, and `x` gets the value from before the increment. The same happens when `inner` tees or stores into a local, global, struct field or memory location that the intervening statement reads or overwrites (read-after-write and write-after-write order). The result is silently wrong code at O2. The check also needs `expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)`, a write-write overlap test, and rejection when `expr_mr.calls` is set.

findings.summary: A call that reads none of the tracked locals, globals, heap or memory counts as 'read-free' and is never marked `may_trap`, so a call in the initializer can be moved past another call (or past effectful or trapping statements) and the two calls swap order.
findings.detail: `may_clobber` reports a clobber for an intervening call only if `!other.is_read_free()`. `is_read_free` ignores `calls`, and a callee reads arbitrary state. Calls also leave `may_trap` false even though a callee can panic or hit `unreachable`. So with `self = struct.new Box{ value: next_id() }; println("x"); use(self.value)`, where both calls have constant arguments: the intervening `println` call is Linear, does not read `self`, and `may_clobber` returns false because the initializer is 'read-free'. The trap check passes because neither call is marked `may_trap`. `next_id()` is then called after `println`, which changes the order of observable I/O and state changes. The same gap lets a trapping intervening statement (for example a division) be reordered ahead of a call that has visible side effects, so output that should come before the trap is lost. A summary with `calls` set should count as reading and writing everything and as possibly trapping.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that can_move_past checks only one direction and that a call in the initializer can be moved past an intervening read of a global it mutates, which is exactly the known defect.

findings.summary: `can_move_past` checks only one direction: whether the intervening statement clobbers what the inner reads. It never checks whether the inner's own writes or calls clobber what the intervening statement reads, so state accesses can be reordered.
findings.detail: The relaxed pass no longer requires the field initializer to be pure, so the inner may contain a `Call`, a `LocalSet`/`LocalTee` or a `GlobalSet`. `can_move_past` only calls `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)` and never the reverse, `expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)`. Two examples: the inner `{ tmp = g(); ... }` moved past `y = tmp`, or the inner `call h()` (h writes global G) moved past `y = global.get G`. In both, the intervening statement now reads the value after the inner ran instead of before. Before this change, adjacency plus the leftmost-use check ruled this out.

findings.summary: A call inside the inner expression is not treated as reading everything, so the inner can be moved past heap, memory or global writes that the callee depends on.
findings.detail: `may_clobber` gives `calls` the 'touches anything' treatment only on the writer side (`self.calls`). When the inner is, say, `call g()` and g reads global G, the heap or linear memory, the inner summary has `calls = true` but empty read sets. An intervening `global.set G`, `struct.set` or `i32.store` then passes every check. The call runs after the write instead of before and returns a different value.

findings.summary: The trap-ordering check ignores calls and other observable side effects in the inner, so output can be lost or duplicated when the intervening statement traps.
findings.detail: `can_move_past` rejects only when both sides have `may_trap`. A `Call` does not set `may_trap`, and it is not treated as an observable effect. Take an inner `call print_and_return()` moved past an intervening `struct.set`, array store or division, which can trap and writes nothing the inner reads. In the original order the output is produced and then the program traps. After the rewrite it traps first and the output is lost. The reverse case also breaks: the inner may trap after the intervening statement has performed an external effect that never ran originally.

findings.summary: Write-after-write ordering on the same local or global is not checked.
findings.detail: No condition compares `expr_mr.local_writes`/`global_writes` with `int_mr.local_writes`/`global_writes`. If the inner writes local or global X, for example via a `Block` containing `LocalSet x` or via `LocalTee`, and the intervening statement also writes X, moving the inner past it swaps the two stores. X then ends with the wrong final value.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that can_move_past checks only int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr) and not the reverse, so an inner call writing a global can be moved past a read of that global, which is exactly the known defect.

findings.summary: `can_move_past` checks only one direction: whether the intervening statement clobbers what the moved initializer reads. It never checks whether the initializer's own writes affect what the intervening statement reads or writes.
findings.detail: This pass does not require the inner field initializer to be pure. It can contain `LocalSet`/`LocalTee`, `GlobalSet`, `StructSet`/`ArraySet`, memory stores or calls. `can_move_past` only calls `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)`. The reverse test (`expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)`) and the write-after-write test are both missing. Example: `self = struct.new Box{ block { tmp = 1; global.set G ...; v } }; y = tmp; use(self.value)`. The intervening `y = tmp` used to run after the initializer and saw the new `tmp`/`G`. After the rewrite it runs first and sees the old values, so the program computes a wrong result. The same happens when both statements write the same local or global: the final value comes out reversed.

findings.summary: When the moved initializer contains a call, `may_clobber` reports no conflict, because a call adds nothing to the read sets.
findings.detail: `may_clobber` treats `calls` as "touches everything" only when the call is on the clobbering side (`self.calls`). If the inner initializer is `Call{..}` with constant or local arguments, its `heap.reads`, `global_reads` and `memory.reads` are all false or empty, even though the callee may read any heap object, global or memory. So an intervening `struct.set`, `global.set` or memory store passes the check, and the call is moved after it. The callee then reads the newly written state instead of the old state, which is a miscompile. The same gap hides the callee's writes from the reverse direction (see the previous finding).

findings.summary: Calls (and `ArrayClone` with a copy helper) are never marked `may_trap`, so the trap-ordering rule in `can_move_past` lets an initializer with side effects or traps be reordered with a trapping intervening statement.
findings.detail: Rule 3 rejects the move only if both summaries have `may_trap` set. A `Call` does not set `may_trap`, yet the callee can trap and can perform host I/O such as printing. Example: `self = struct.new Box{ call log_and_get() }; y = struct.get(r).f; use(self.value)`. Here the intervening `struct.get` traps on null, and the initializer's call printed before that trap in the original order. After the move the trap fires first and the output is lost. If the callee itself traps, the intervening statement's effects now happen before that trap, which also changes observable behaviour. Rule 3 also ignores side effects that the inner initializer performs before an intervening trap even when no call is involved.

findings.summary: `find_use_site` never checks the control-flow effect of the inner initializer, so an initializer that can branch or return is moved past intervening statements that it used to skip.
findings.detail: `can_move_past` requires only the intervening statement to have `Control::Linear`. The control field of `expr_mr` is ignored. If the field initializer is a block that can `return`, `br` out, or hit `unreachable`, the original program exits before the intervening statements run. After the rewrite those statements (for example `global.set`, `struct.set` or a local copy) run before the exit, so their side effects become visible when they should not. The old pass was safe only because def and use were adjacent, and this PR removes that guarantee.

grade.reason: Finding 0 says `can_move_past` checks only whether the intervening statement clobbers the moved initializer, and that the reverse check `expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)` is missing, which is exactly the fixed defect.

entries.defect: inflate_get_gzip_header converted each FNAME/FCOMMENT byte to its own char (Latin-1 style), while gzip_compress_with_header wrote the names' UTF-8 bytes, so non-ASCII names and comments came back as mojibake.

findings.summary: Zlib streams written with a preset dictionary do not follow the zlib format: the dictionary bytes are compressed into the stream and the Adler-32 trailer covers dictionary + data.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_zlib` with `has_dict` deflates `dict ++ input` and writes `adler32(combined)` as the trailer. A real preset dictionary only primes the LZ77 window; it is never part of the compressed data, and the trailer covers the uncompressed data only. When zlib/zlib-rs inflates this stream with the dictionary (after Z_NEED_DICT), the output starts with the dictionary bytes and the trailer check fails. The same stream given to `inflate_zlib`/`uncompress` also breaks: they ignore the FDICT bit and try to decode the 4-byte DICTID as deflate data. Nothing in Wado can read this output except Wado's own `InflateStream` with the same dictionary.

findings.summary: In RAW_FORMAT, a DeflateStream with a dictionary puts the dictionary bytes into the output.
findings.detail: `compress_raw` with `has_dict` returns `deflate_with_level(dict ++ input)`. Any raw inflater, including Wado's own `inflate_raw` or `InflateStream` in RAW_FORMAT, returns the dictionary followed by the data instead of just the data. The decompressed result is wrong, and the dictionary costs space instead of improving compression.

findings.summary: `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` never checks the DICTID, and it cannot decode real zlib preset-dictionary streams.
findings.detail: With FDICT set, it skips the 4-byte DICTID without comparing it to `adler32(self.dict)`, inflates with an empty window, then drops the first `dict.len()` output bytes. If the caller passes a dictionary of a different length than the one used to compress, the call silently returns wrong data: the Adler check covers the combined buffer, so it still passes. Real zlib FDICT streams refer back into the dictionary with distances beyond the start of the output. Those references are invalid without a primed window, so such streams fail or decode wrongly.

findings.summary: The lazy-matching path inserts the current position into the hash chain twice, so it links to itself and the older chain is lost.
findings.detail: In the "previous match was better" branch, `pos` was already inserted earlier in the same iteration (`prev[pos%32768]=head[h]; head[h]=pos`). The loop `for i in 0..skip-1` then starts at i=0 and inserts `pos` again, which sets `prev[pos] = head[h] = pos`. Every later chain walk that reaches `pos` spins on that entry until `max_chain` runs out and never sees older candidates, and position `pos+skip-1` is never inserted. Levels 4-9 therefore miss matches and compress noticeably worse than intended.

findings.summary: `uncompress2` enforces `max_output` only after decompressing the whole input.
findings.detail: `uncompress2` calls `uncompress(input)`, which builds the full output, and only then compares its length with `max_output`. A small malicious input (a decompression bomb) can still use unbounded memory and time before the limit is checked, so the limit gives no protection.

grade.reason: No finding mentions how the gzip header FNAME/FCOMMENT bytes are decoded or the UTF-8 versus Latin-1 mismatch; the findings cover the dictionary, lazy matching, and uncompress2 instead.

findings.summary: Compressing with a preset dictionary (`DeflateStream::compress_zlib` with `has_dict`) writes the dictionary bytes into the compressed stream and puts their checksum in the trailer, so the output is not valid zlib FDICT data.
findings.detail: The code prepends the dictionary to the input, deflates `dict+input` as literals and matches, and writes `adler32(dict+input)` as the trailer. In real zlib, the dictionary only preloads the LZ77 window: the stream encodes only the input, and the trailer covers only the input. A standard inflater such as zlib, zlib-rs or flate2, given the same dictionary through inflateSetDictionary, decodes the dictionary text followed by the data. Its checksum check passes, so it silently returns the wrong data. The new cross-validation test only checks that the FDICT bit is set, which is why this was not caught.

findings.summary: `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` cannot decode standard zlib streams that use a preset dictionary.
findings.detail: When FDICT is set, the code skips the DICTID without comparing it to `adler32(self.dict)`. It inflates with an empty window, so the dictionary is never loaded. It then checks the adler over the raw output and cuts `dict.len()` bytes off the front. A stream made by real zlib with a dictionary contains back-references into the dictionary, which fail as invalid distances, and its adler covers only the payload, so it panics or returns truncated or corrupt data. A wrong dictionary is never detected either. It only round-trips with Wado's own non-standard encoder.

findings.summary: `DeflateStream::compress_raw` with a dictionary produces raw deflate data that decompresses to the dictionary followed by the input.
findings.detail: In RAW_FORMAT the dictionary is prepended to the input and the whole buffer is deflated. Any raw inflater, including Wado's own `InflateStream` in RAW_FORMAT, which never strips a prefix, returns `dict+data` instead of `data`, so the result is wrong.

findings.summary: In lazy matching (levels 4-9), emitting a deferred match inserts the current position into the hash chain a second time, creating a self-loop `prev[pos] = pos`.
findings.detail: In the `match_available` branch the search at `pos` has already done `prev[pos] = head[h]; head[h] = pos`. The following loop `for i = 0; i < skip - 1` starts at `i = 0`, so it inserts `pos` again, and `head[h]` is now `pos`, which makes `prev[pos] = pos`. Any later chain walk that reaches `pos` keeps revisiting it until `max_chain` runs out (up to 4096 iterations of up to 258-byte comparisons at level 9). Older candidates are never examined, so compression gets worse and CPU time is wasted. The insertion should start at `i = 1`, as the immediate-emit branch does.

findings.summary: `uncompress2` only checks `max_output` after decompressing the whole input, so the limit does not bound memory or work.
findings.detail: `uncompress2` calls `uncompress(input)` in full and only then compares `result.len()` with `max_output`. A small malicious input such as a deflate bomb can therefore expand without limit before the panic, which defeats the purpose of an output size limit on untrusted data.

findings.summary: `inflate_get_gzip_header` corrupts file names and comments that contain non-ASCII bytes.
findings.detail: `bytes_to_string` turns each byte into a `char` and appends it as a string. Bytes 0x80-0xFF become code points U+0080-U+00FF and are re-encoded as two UTF-8 bytes. A name written by `gzip_compress_with_header` (which writes the raw bytes of the String) therefore does not survive a round trip when it contains UTF-8, such as Japanese file names.

grade.reason: Finding 5 identifies that bytes_to_string maps each byte to its own char, so UTF-8 names and comments written by gzip_compress_with_header do not round-trip, which is exactly the known defect.

findings.summary: Compressing with a preset dictionary puts the dictionary bytes into the compressed data and into the checksum, so the stream does not follow the zlib FDICT format.
findings.detail: DeflateStream::compress_zlib joins dict and input, deflates the joined buffer, and writes adler32(dict+input) as the trailer. In real zlib the dictionary only primes the LZ77 window: it is never emitted, and the trailer covers only the input. A standard inflater given the dictionary therefore returns dict+data, with the dictionary bytes wrongly in front. The output is also no smaller, because the dictionary is encoded as ordinary data instead of being matched against.

findings.summary: InflateStream::decompress_zlib cannot decode real zlib streams that use a preset dictionary, and it accepts a wrong dictionary without error.
findings.detail: When FDICT is set, the code checks that a dictionary was given, skips the 4-byte DICTID without comparing it to adler32(dict), and inflates with an empty window. It then drops the first dict.len() bytes of the output. A stream from real zlib or zlib-rs with FDICT has back-references into the dictionary, so decoding fails or produces garbage, and real data gets cut off. For streams made by Wado itself, any dictionary of the same length is accepted and nothing reports the mismatch.

findings.summary: A RAW_FORMAT DeflateStream with a dictionary writes the dictionary into the output data.
findings.detail: compress_raw deflates dict+input and adds no marker. The raw format carries no FDICT flag, and InflateStream in RAW_FORMAT ignores the dictionary. Decompressing therefore returns the dictionary bytes followed by the data, so the round trip loses data integrity in Wado and with any other raw inflater.

findings.summary: In lazy matching, the hash insertion after emitting the earlier match is off by one: it makes a self-loop in the hash chain and leaves one position out.
findings.detail: In the 'previous match was better' branch, position pos is already in the hash table, but the loop runs i = 0..skip-2. That inserts pos a second time, so prev[pos] = head[h] = pos, a self-loop. The last position the match covers (pos+skip-1) is never inserted. Later chain walks that reach pos spin on it until max_chain runs out and never reach older candidates. Levels 4-9 lose matches, and compression is worse than it should be.

findings.summary: inflate_get_gzip_header changes the bytes of any non-ASCII file name or comment.
findings.detail: bytes_to_string adds each byte as `{buf[i] as char}`. A byte of 0x80 or above becomes the Unicode code point U+0080..U+00FF and is stored as two UTF-8 bytes. A UTF-8 or Latin-1 name such as 'café.txt' comes back as mojibake, and gzip_compress_with_header writes it out differently, so the header does not survive a round trip.

findings.summary: gzip_compress_with_header writes a corrupt header when the extra field is longer than 65535 bytes.
findings.detail: XLEN is written as (xlen & 0xFFFF) while all xlen bytes are still appended. With an extra field over 65535 bytes, a reader skips only XLEN mod 65536 bytes and reads the rest of the extra data as the name, comment or deflate stream, so the whole gzip member is corrupt. zlib limits or rejects such headers; this code checks nothing.

grade.reason: Finding 4 says bytes_to_string casts each byte to its own char, so non-ASCII names and comments come back as mojibake, which is the same root cause as the known defect.
