entries.defect: write_atomic named its temp file only by process id, so concurrent threads in one process writing the same cache path shared one temp file and could rename it out from under each other, causing failed writes.

findings.summary: The options descriptor for a registry generator uses the WIT kebab-case field and enum-case names, so a multi-word option field or enum value cannot be supplied at the use site.
findings.detail: `record_descriptor` copies `field.name` and `options_type` copies the enum `cases` names straight from the decoded WIT. Those names are CM kebab-case, e.g. `max-depth` or `very-fast`. `options_check::validate` matches the user's `options: { max_depth: 3 }` keys and enum strings exactly against the descriptor. A Wado identifier key `max_depth` is therefore reported as an unknown field, and the required `max-depth` as missing. Enum values written with their Wado names fail the same way. A path-built generator accepts these exact options because its descriptor carries Wado names, and the runtime converts to kebab itself (`canonical_to_val` calls `to_kebab`). Only single-word fields, such as gale's `highlight` and `trace`, work.

findings.summary: A registry generator component is pulled and executed without checking it against the `integrity` digest that `wado update` records in `wado.lock`.
findings.detail: `wado update` writes a `[[build-dependency]]` entry with `integrity = sha256:…`. However, `resolve_spec`, `build_dep::fetch_build_dependencies` and `try_read_spec_cache` all pull by mutable tag (`world_reference(..., &version)`) or read the cache file. None of them compares the bytes or manifest digest with the locked integrity. If the tag is re-pushed or the registry is compromised, different generator code is fetched, cached for good and run at build time with no error. The lock's integrity pin has no effect on any build.

findings.summary: `wado fetch` resolves versions live and ignores `wado.lock`, so it can fill the cache with a version other than the locked one that compile/check/LSP look up.
findings.detail: `fetch::run` calls `wado_manifest::resolve`, which picks the highest matching registry version, and caches that version. The compiler and LSP index (`registry_component_needs` / `dependency_index_from`) look up the version pinned in `wado.lock`. Once a newer matching version is published, `wado fetch` caches the new one. `wado check`, `query` and the LSP keep reporting "… is not cached; run `wado fetch`", and running `wado fetch` again never fixes it.

findings.summary: A locked generator version is used even when it no longer satisfies the `[build-dependencies]` requirement, so a requirement change is silently ignored until `wado update`.
findings.detail: `resolve_build_dependencies` and `CliGeneratorProvider::resolve_version` return `locked_versions.get(package)` as soon as one exists. They never check it against the manifest's `version` requirement or the lock's `deps-hash`. For example, if a user changes `"wado-lang:gale" = { version = "^0.1.0" }` while the lock still says 0.0.9, compile and fetch keep using 0.0.9 with no warning or diagnostic.

grade.reason: None of the findings addresses write_atomic's pid-only temp file name causing concurrent same-process writers to collide; they cover option naming, integrity checks, lock handling in fetch, and version requirement drift.

findings.summary: For registry generators, the options descriptor rebuilt from the component WIT uses kebab-case field and enum-case names, so use-site options with Wado names fail to validate.
findings.detail: `record_descriptor` copies `field.name` and `options_type` copies the enum `case.name` straight from wit-parser, which produces kebab-case names (`max-depth`, `high-contrast`). The use-site validator (`options_check::validate` and `check_value` for `Enum`) compares names exactly. The runtime does the opposite: `kiln_runtime::canonical_to_val` expects raw Wado identifiers and converts them with `to_kebab`. A registry generator whose `Options` has a multi-word field such as `max_depth` therefore rejects `options: { max_depth: 3 }` with "unknown options field" and then reports `max-depth` as a missing required field. Likewise, an enum value written as `"HighContrast"` is rejected because the variant list only holds `high-contrast`. The same options work when the generator comes from a path dependency. Only single-word names, like gale's `highlight`/`trace`, get through.

findings.summary: Registry generators are pulled by mutable tag and cached without any check against the lock's `integrity` digest, so the pin does not protect what runs.
findings.detail: `wado update` now writes an `integrity` manifest digest into each `[[build-dependency]]`. `resolve_spec` never reads it: it pulls with `oci::world_reference(..., &version)` (a tag) and stores the bytes in the shared `~/wado` cache. `try_read_spec_cache` then trusts whatever file sits at that path from then on. `wado fetch` (`fetch_build_dependencies`) does the same. If a tag is moved or the registry is compromised, the component that runs at compile time differs from the locked one and nothing reports it. Planting a file in the shared cache also takes over every project that uses that coordinate and version.

findings.summary: The locked generator version is used even when it no longer satisfies the `[build-dependencies]` requirement, so a stale lock silently picks the old generator.
findings.detail: `resolve_build_dependencies` and `CliGeneratorProvider::resolve_version` take the version from `locked_generator_versions` as soon as the coordinate appears in `wado.lock`, without checking it against the manifest's `version` requirement. `deps_hash` now covers build-dependencies, but nothing ever compares it with the lock (`Manifest::deps_hash` is only called by `update`). If a user changes `"wado-lang:gale" = { version = "^0.1" }` and does not run `wado update`, compile, check and fetch keep using 0.0.9 with no warning. The lock map is also keyed only by `ns:pkg`, ignoring the registry, so a generator declared against another registry, or inline in single-file mode, can pick up the wrong pin.

findings.summary: `wado check` and `wado query` are documented as the offline tier, yet a registry generator still lists tags and pulls over the network during the Kiln pipeline.
findings.detail: `attach_manifest_and_component_deps(..., false)` keeps library components offline. However, `check.rs` also builds a `CliGeneratorProvider` with a full `RegistryContext`. On a cache miss, `resolve_spec` calls `oci::list_tags` (when there is no lock pin) and `oci::pull_component`. A cold cache therefore makes `check` hit the registry, or fail with a fetch error when offline, instead of giving the `wado fetch` hint that the offline design promises.

grade.reason: None of the findings mention write_atomic's temp file being named only by pid, or the race between threads writing the same cache path that this causes.

findings.summary: Options recovered from a registry generator's WIT keep the kebab-case field and enum-case names, so any multi-word option field or enum case cannot be written at the use site.
findings.detail: `record_descriptor` copies `field.name` straight from the WIT (for example `max-depth`), and `options_type` copies enum cases the same way (for example `high-contrast`). `options_check::validate` compares the keys written in `options: { … }` (Wado identifiers such as `max_depth`) with the descriptor names exactly, so it reports an unknown field and then a missing required field. Enum values written with their Wado name (`HighContrast`) fail `variants.iter().any(|v| v == s)` for the same reason. `kiln_runtime::canonical_to_val` expects raw Wado names and converts them to kebab-case itself, so the descriptor should hold Wado names. Today only single-word options such as gale's `highlight`/`trace` work.

findings.summary: `write_atomic` names its temp file only by process id, so two concurrent writers in the same process can publish a half-written `component.wasm` that the `is_file()` check then trusts permanently.
findings.detail: The temp path is `component.tmp-<pid>`. Concurrent compiles in one process (for example `wado test` compiling fixtures in parallel, or two tasks pulling the same generator or component) share that path. Writer A finishes writing and renames the temp file into place while writer B is truncating and rewriting the same inode, so the published file is partly written. B's rename then fails with ENOENT. `dep_component::pull_component`, `fetch.rs` and `fetch_build_dependencies` all skip the download when `is_file()` is true, so the corrupt cache entry is never repaired. The comment claims this case is safe, but it is not.

findings.summary: The generator `integrity` digest written to `wado.lock` is never checked when the generator component is pulled or read from the cache, even though that code then runs during the build.
findings.detail: `wado update` records the sub-path manifest digest as `integrity`, but `locked_generator_versions` reads only the version. `resolve_spec` and `fetch_build_dependencies` pull `world_reference(..., version)` by tag and run whatever bytes they get. If a tag is re-pushed or the registry is compromised, different generator code runs at compile time while the lock appears to pin a digest. The library components in `dep_component::pull_component` are not checked against their lock integrity either.

findings.summary: `resolve_version` uses the `wado.lock` pin, or an explicit `@version` in the module specifier, without checking it against the `[build-dependencies]` version requirement, so a stale lock silently selects the wrong generator version.
findings.detail: `resolve_version` returns `pin` first and then `locked_versions.get(package)`, and never compares either with `req`. Nothing checks the lock's `deps-hash` against the manifest. After editing `"wado-lang:gale" = { version = "^0.1" }`, builds keep using the 0.0.9 entry from the old lock and give no error. A `module: "ns:gen@9.9.9"` likewise bypasses the declared requirement. The lock lookup is also keyed by the bare coordinate, ignoring the registry URL, so two registries hosting the same coordinate share one pin.

findings.summary: In inline mode, a `lib:` nickname with no matching build-dependency is fetched as if `lib:nick` were a real registry coordinate.
findings.detail: When `parts.key` is not found in `build_dependencies`, the `else` branch sets `package = parts.key`. For `module: "lib:gale"` with an inline `registry`, or with `[registries].default` set, that means pulling `<registry>/lib/gale/core-kiln-generator`. `lib:` is a reserved alias namespace and is never a published coordinate, so the user gets a confusing registry or network error, or the wrong artifact if one exists there, instead of a diagnostic saying the nickname is undeclared.

findings.summary: On the build tier, every compile of a project whose `wado.lock` does not pin every registry dependency now does a live network resolve, and a failure aborts the compile.
findings.detail: `manifest_and_component_index` calls `fetch_component_dependencies` whenever any registry `[dependencies]` entry exists. If any lock-pinned need is missing, this falls back to `fetch_via_resolve`, which runs a full `wado_manifest::resolve` with registry tag listings. Any error becomes "Error fetching component dependencies" and fails the compile, even for entry files that never import the dependency (for example each fixture under `wado test`). Before this change such files compiled offline.

grade.reason: Finding 1 says write_atomic names its temp file only by pid, so concurrent writers in one process share the temp file and B's rename fails with ENOENT, which is the same root cause as the known defect.

entries.defect: When a provider's dependency was dead-code-eliminated and never added to dep_instances, compose_dependency_components bailed with 'no composed dependency imports provider interface' instead of skipping the unused provider, so compilation failed.

findings.summary: Every world-level function of a dependency is imported as a component func, but its signature is converted with a converter that handles only primitives and string, so any other type makes the compiler panic.
findings.detail: `generate_cm_world_func_imports` calls `wado_type_to_cm_val_type` with empty enum/flags/borrow maps and `None` for the stream and result indices. Any parameter or result type other than a primitive or `String` hits `panic!("unsupported Wado param type for CM")` or `expect("result param type not defined")`. That covers `list<T>`, `option<T>`, `result`, records, enums and tuples. The doc comment says such signatures are "rejected", but no check does that. Before this change `build_bindings` returned a clean error for world-function exports. `resolve_import_plan` (Phase 4) also pushes every registered world function, not just the called ones. So importing any item from a component that has one such world function crashes the compiler, even when that function is never called.

findings.summary: A provider whose dependency is not in the import plan makes composition fail with a panic instead of a diagnostic.
findings.detail: `compose_dependency_components` only puts a dependency into `dep_instances` when it supplies a planned interface or world function. A `with { provider: ... }` import is compiled into `options.providers` whether or not the dependency is called. If the dependency is never used, or is only used in code that is dropped from this build (for example test blocks in a non-test compile), the provider loop finds no importer and calls `anyhow::bail!("no composed dependency imports provider interface")`. The outer `match compose()` turns that into `panic!("failed to compose CM component dependencies")`. The same panic happens when two `use` declarations both name a provider for the same dependency interface: the second `graph.connect` targets an import that is already connected.

findings.summary: Calls to world-level functions from a dependency skip the effect requirement that interface calls get, so the dependency's WASI and guest-effect imports are neither checked nor listed as imports.
findings.detail: `effect_op_requirement` only rebuilds the dependency's host-leaf requirements for `#[cm]` interface ops. A world function is a free function, and its adapter's effects are explicitly cleared in `generate_import_adapters`. `register_component_decls` also records host-leaf imports only for interface FQs. On top of that, `imported_cm_interface_fqs` adds nothing for `ImportKind::WorldFunction`, on the assumption that the dependency is pure. So when a dependency's world function needs `wasi:cli/...` or a guest-effect interface, the consumer compiles with no missing-effect error, and its declared import list leaves out interfaces the composed component still imports. Any non-WASI guest import is left unsatisfied.

findings.summary: The LSP always passes an empty provider set to `check_semantics`, so in the editor every file that uses `with { provider: ... }` shows a false "missing effect" error.
findings.detail: In the batch compiler, a supplied provider removes the dependency's guest-effect requirement through `provided_import_fqs`. The LSP passes `IndexSet::default()` and never reads the `provider` attribute. For example, `Hlc::wrap(...)` in `provider_surface.wado` compiles fine, but the editor reports `missing effect 'Highlight' required by 'Hlc::wrap'`. The provider FQ is known statically: it is the dependency's single non-WASI host-leaf import.

findings.summary: `register_lib_guest_effect_imports` rejects any `--lib` whose entry module has an interface that kebab-cases to the package's interface name, even when that effect is handled inside the library and never becomes an import.
findings.detail: The collision check runs over every non-`#[cm]` interface in the entry module before usage is known. A library such as package `highlight` with an internal `interface Highlight`, handled with `with &mut h do { ... }`, compiled fine before this change. It now fails with a DuplicateDefinition "collides with the library's own interface name" error, even though no import FQ would ever be minted for it.

findings.summary: An interface satisfied by a provider is still reported as a surviving import in `imported_cm_interfaces`, so the embedded WIT/world claims an import the composed component does not have.
findings.detail: For `ImportKind::Component`, `imported_cm_interface_fqs` adds every `host_leaf_imports_for(fq)` without filtering out FQs that providers satisfy. Effect-check discharges these FQs and codegen composes them away, as the test asserting the composed component no longer imports `highlight` shows. The flat import list that the WIT producer reads still includes `test:hlc/highlight@0.1.0`, so the component's declared contract does not match its real imports.

findings.summary: World-level function imports are keyed only by their bare name, so two dependencies exporting a function with the same name overwrite each other's entries.
findings.detail: `register_world_import` puts the function into `effect_to_func`/`world_import_functions` under `func_name`, and `register_component_decls` writes `world_import_sources[name]` with the last dependency's source. Calls to the first dependency's function then fail the source-equality check in `rewrite_calls_in_expr`/`EffectCallCollector`, so they are never retargeted to an adapter. The local alias `wasi:/::name` is also shared by both functions. The result is an unresolved call, or a composition that connects two exports to one program import (`graph.connect` error, then a panic).

grade.reason: Finding 1 describes the same problem: when the dependency is unused or eliminated it is missing from `dep_instances`, so the provider loop bails with 'no composed dependency imports provider interface' instead of skipping the provider.

findings.summary: The library-name collision check rejects every guest effect interface whose kebab name matches the library's interface name, including effects the library handles itself, so `--lib` packages that used to compile now fail.
findings.detail: `register_lib_guest_effect_imports` runs for every `--lib` build. It errors on any `interface X` with no `#[cm]` methods whose kebab name equals the library's interface segment. It never checks whether that effect is actually left unhandled at the boundary. A package `hltest` that declares `interface Hltest` and handles it internally with `with h do` never imports it, so there is no FQ collision. It still hits the new DuplicateDefinition error and the build aborts. That is a false compile error and a regression.

findings.summary: Inline provider jobs are never de-duplicated, so the same dependency gets one provider per `use ... with { provider }`, and composition then wires two providers into the same import.
findings.detail: `resolve_inline_providers` adds a job for each `use` carrying `provider` in each loaded module. If two modules (or two `use` lines) import the same `.wasm` with a provider, the provider is compiled twice and pushed twice with the same `import_fq`. `compose_dependency_components` then calls `graph.connect` for each provider against the same dependency instance's import index. Once that import is connected, connecting it again should fail in wasm-compose, so a valid program fails during codegen (it also does an extra full compile).

findings.summary: World-level function imports are keyed globally by bare name, so two dependencies exporting the same world function overwrite each other.
findings.detail: `register_world_import` stores the info in `effect_to_func`, `world_import_functions` and `world_import_sources` under the bare snake name. `register_component_decls` overwrites `world_import_sources[name]` with the last dependency. Calls to the first dependency's `highlight` no longer match `world_import_source(&func.name) == Some(&func.module_source)`, so they are not retargeted to an adapter (unresolved call / ICE). Composition also sees `highlight` in both assets' `component_world_func_names` and tries to connect both to the single program import, which fails.

findings.summary: A world-level function's dependency capabilities (its WASI host-leaf imports) are dropped entirely: no effect is required at the call site, and the import is left out of the reported import list.
findings.detail: The world-function adapter's `effects` are cleared. `register_component_decls` records `host_leaf_imports` only per interface FQ, never for world functions. `imported_cm_interface_fqs` skips `WorldFunction` entries on the assumption that the function is pure. A dependency whose only export is a world function but which imports e.g. `wasi:cli/stdout` can therefore be called with no effect diagnostic. Its WASI import still survives composition but is missing from `wir.imported_cm_interfaces`, so the embedded WIT contract is wrong.

findings.summary: World-level functions whose signatures use named types are not rejected as documented, which leads to an ICE/panic later instead of a diagnostic.
findings.detail: `emit_world_function` maps parameter and result types with `current_fq = ""` and records no error for named (record/variant/enum) types, although the comments say such signatures are rejected in v1. `generate_cm_world_func_imports` then calls `wado_type_to_cm_val_type` with empty type maps. A component-defined named type in the signature hits the unresolved-type panics in codegen instead of a clean 'not yet supported' error.

findings.summary: `component_interface_fqs` drops every exported interface that the component also imports, so a pass-through or middleware component that imports and exports the same FQ is never composed.
findings.detail: The new filter removes any export FQ found in the module's host-leaf import list. A component that imports `ns:pkg/iface` and also exports `ns:pkg/iface` (a wrapper/decorator) loses its export classification, so its calls are not planned as a Component import and the dependency is not composed in. `build_bindings` also calls `emit_interface` twice for the same interface, producing duplicate items.

grade.reason: None of the findings flag the bail in compose_dependency_components that fires when a provider's dependency was dead-code-eliminated and is absent from dep_instances; finding 1 looks at the same function but describes a different failure, duplicate providers being connected twice.

findings.summary: A world-level function whose signature uses a list, option, result, tuple or named type now crashes the compiler with a panic, where it used to get a clear error.
findings.detail: `build_bindings` used to reject every world-level function export with a clean error. Now it accepts all of them, and `emit_world_function` maps any WIT type, including `List`, `Option`, `Result` and named records. `generate_cm_world_func_imports` then turns these types into CM types through `wado_type_to_cm_val_type`, passing empty maps and `None` indices. That function panics on `List`/`Option` ("unsupported generic param type"), on `Result` (`result_param_type_idx.expect`) and on any named non-primitive. The doc comment says such signatures are "rejected", but no check does that. So importing, for example, `f: func(x: list<u8>)` is now an internal compiler error instead of a diagnostic.

findings.summary: A `provider` directive on a dependency that the program never calls makes composition panic.
findings.detail: `compose_dependency_components` builds `dep_instances` only from assets whose interfaces or functions are in the import plan, which means the program uses them. Every provider is then wired unconditionally, and when no composed dependency imports its interface the code does `bail!("no composed dependency imports provider interface ...")`. All composition errors end in `panic!("failed to compose CM component dependencies")`. So `use { Hlc } from "./hlc.wasm" with { provider: ... }`, where `Hlc` is unused or only used in code that is filtered out, crashes the compiler instead of compiling or giving a diagnostic.

findings.summary: For a dependency that exports only world-level functions, the dependency's own imports (WASI capabilities or guest effects) are never recorded, so effect checking and the import list ignore them.
findings.detail: `register_component_decls` stores `component_host_leaf_imports` only per interface FQ. World functions get just a `world_import_sources` entry. On top of that, `generate_import_adapters` clears the adapter's effects, and `imported_cm_interface_fqs` ignores `WorldFunction` entries because it treats them as pure. If such a dependency imports `wasi:filesystem` or a guest interface, the consumer calls it without being required to hold the matching effect, so the missing-effect diagnostic never fires. The leftover imports of the composed component are also missing from `imported_cm_interfaces` (the WIT contract), so the requirement goes unchecked and the component can fail at instantiation.

findings.summary: The same provider interface can be collected and wired twice, which makes composition panic.
findings.detail: `resolve_inline_providers` makes one job per `use ... with { provider }` in every loaded module, with no deduplication by dependency or FQ. If two modules import the same dependency with a provider, two `ProviderComponent`s with the same `import_fq` are composed. Both try to `graph.connect` into the same dependency import slot. wasm-compose rejects connecting an import twice, and that error is turned into a compiler panic.

grade.reason: Finding 1 says compose_dependency_components bails with 'no composed dependency imports provider interface' when the dependency is unused or filtered out. That is exactly the known defect.

entries.defect: walk_and_delete propagated NotFound errors from read_dir, the directory entries, file_type and remove_file, so a file or directory removed concurrently during output reconcile aborted the whole pipeline with an I/O error.

findings.summary: The generator's `host::read-file` import can read any file on the host: absolute paths and `..` paths are passed straight through to `load_source`.
findings.detail: `KilnHostState::read_file` passes the path the generator supplies directly to `self.host.load_source(&path)`. For the CLI, that is `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, which does `base_path.join(path)`. `Path::join` with an absolute path such as `/home/u/.ssh/id_rsa`, or with `../../..`, leaves the project root. A third-party generator from `[build-dependencies]`, supposed to be sandboxed with only two host imports, can therefore read any file the user can read and copy its contents into the generated outputs. Nothing checks that the path stays inside the manifest root.

findings.summary: The cache check ignores the generator identity, so changing `module` (for example bumping the generator version) still counts as a cache hit and keeps the outputs of the old generator.
findings.detail: `run_pipeline` reuses a prior entry when `options_hash` matches and `cache_matches` succeeds. `cache_matches` compares only the primary file, the inputs, the reads and the output hashes. It never compares `entry.generator` with `generator_identity(&invocation.module)`, and no generator source hash is checked either. If a user changes `module = "ns:proto@1.0.0"` to `@2.0.0` without touching the schemas, the old generated code is silently kept and the old entry is written back to `wado.lock`.

findings.summary: Changing an invocation's `output-dir` still counts as a cache hit, so no files are generated in the new directory.
findings.detail: `cache_matches` checks the recorded output paths, which are still in the old directory and still exist with matching hashes. It never checks that they lie under `invocation.output_dir`. The generator is therefore skipped. The kept paths are filed under the new directory key, which is empty or missing, and the lockfile goes on pointing at the old location. A consumer resolving from the new `output-dir` finds nothing until some input changes.

findings.summary: A generator output path that contains `.` segments or backslashes is recorded under a different normalized path than the file actually written, so `reconcile_outputs` deletes the file it just wrote.
findings.detail: `validate_rel_output_path` accepts `CurDir` components such as `a/./b.wado` and Unix backslash filenames such as `a\b.wado`. The file is written at the real path (`a/b.wado`, or a file literally named `a\b.wado`). The recorded path comes from `InvocationPath::normalize`, which keeps `/./` in the middle of a path and turns `\` into `/`. `walk_and_delete` then compares the real relative path from `read_dir` against these kept strings, finds no match, and deletes the freshly generated file because it carries the `#![generated]` marker. `cache_matches` also looks for the output at the normalized path, so every later run is a cache miss.

findings.summary: Generator diagnostics go to the inner LSP host, so the CLI never prints them to stderr.
findings.detail: `run_generator` passes `self.inner.clone()` (the `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost`) to `kiln_runtime::run_generator`, and `relay_diagnostic` calls `emit_diagnostic` on that inner host. The inner host only appends to its buffer. The outer `FilesystemCompilerHost::emit_diagnostic`, which prints to stderr and applies the log-level filter, is bypassed. Errors and warnings a generator reports through `host::emit-diagnostic` are never shown to the user.

findings.summary: A read of a missing file is reported to the generator as `io(...)`, never as `not-found`.
findings.detail: `read_file` maps only `SourceError::NotFound` to `HostError::NotFound`. The CLI's `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source` returns `SourceError::IoError` for every failure, including a missing file. A generator that probes for optional includes and treats `not-found` as benign gets a generic I/O error instead and may abort. Failed reads are also not recorded, so creating the file later does not invalidate the cache.

grade.reason: No finding addresses walk_and_delete aborting on NotFound errors from concurrent removal; finding 3 concerns walk_and_delete wrongly deleting files because normalized paths mismatch, which is a different root cause.

findings.summary: A cache hit never checks the generator identity, so outputs from an old generator version are reused after the module version changes.
findings.detail: `run_pipeline` finds the prior entry by invocation name and only filters on `options_hash`. `cache_matches` then compares the primary, inputs, reads and outputs, but never `entry.generator` against `generator_identity(&invocation.module)`, and the component bytes are never hashed. If `module` changes from `ns:proto@1.0.0` to `ns:proto@2.0.0` (or a different generator) while the schemas and options stay the same, the pipeline reports the entry as cached and keeps the files the old generator produced.

findings.summary: Generator `read-file` calls go straight to the host's `load_source`, so a sandboxed generator can read any file on the machine.
findings.detail: `KilnHostState::read_file` passes the guest-supplied path unchanged to `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, which does `base_path.join(path)`. An absolute path replaces the base, and `..` segments walk out of it. A third-party generator can therefore read `/etc/passwd`, `~/.ssh/id_rsa` and similar files, and copy the contents into its generated output. This breaks the sandboxing the WIT world is meant to provide.

findings.summary: With the real CLI host, a missing file is never reported to the generator as `not-found`.
findings.detail: `read_file` returns `HostError::NotFound` only for `SourceError::NotFound`. The CLI's `FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source` turns every `std::fs::read` failure, including ENOENT, into `SourceError::IoError`. A generator that probes include paths and expects `not-found` instead gets `io(...)`. It will likely treat that as a hard error and fail.

findings.summary: Failed reads are not recorded, so a file that appears later at a probed path does not invalidate the cache.
findings.detail: Only successful `load_source` results are pushed to `reads`. If a generator looks for a file on an include path, finds nothing and falls back to something else, nothing records that lookup. If the user later creates the file, `cache_matches` still returns a hit and the stale output is kept.

findings.summary: Diagnostics from generators are sent to the inner LSP host and never printed by the CLI.
findings.detail: `run_generator` passes `self.inner.clone()`, the inner `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost`, to `kiln_runtime::run_generator`, and `relay_diagnostic` calls `emit_diagnostic` on that inner host. The outer host's `emit_diagnostic`, which prints to stderr and applies the log-level filter, is skipped. Generator errors and warnings are therefore only collected, never shown to the user. Generator diagnostics at `Error` level also do not fail the run.

findings.summary: When one invocation's output directory contains another's, reconcile deletes the inner invocation's freshly generated files.
findings.detail: `kept_by_dir` is keyed by each invocation's exact `output_dir`, and `walk_and_delete` recurses into every subdirectory. Suppose invocation A uses `output-dir = "gen"` and B uses `gen/b`. Reconciling A walks into `gen/b`, finds B's `#![generated]` files missing from A's kept list, and deletes them. The lockfile still records them as current outputs.

findings.summary: A generator that reads files by absolute path causes a cache miss on every run.
findings.detail: `build_cache_entry` stores read paths through `InvocationPath::normalize`, which drops empty segments and so strips the leading `/` (`/abs/x` becomes `abs/x`). `cache_matches` then loads that relative path, the load fails, and the result is always a miss. The generator is re-executed on every build.

findings.summary: `output_dir` from the manifest is not checked, so generated files can be written outside the project.
findings.detail: `lower` only normalizes `output_dir`, which keeps `..` segments and absolute paths (as relative but still joinable). `execute` writes to `manifest_root.join(output_dir)`, and `reconcile_outputs` deletes files under that directory. The per-file path inside the directory is validated, but the directory itself is not, so `output-dir = "../.."` lets generator output and stale-file deletion reach outside the project root.

grade.reason: None of the findings mention walk_and_delete failing with NotFound errors when files or directories are removed concurrently during reconcile; finding 5 concerns walk_and_delete but is about nested output directories being deleted.

findings.summary: A cached result is reused after the generator module changes, because the cache check never compares the recorded generator identity.
findings.detail: `run_pipeline` only requires the cached entry's `options_hash` to match before calling `cache_matches`. `cache_matches` then checks the primary file, inputs, reads and outputs, but never compares `entry.generator` with `generator_identity(&invocation.module)`. Suppose a user bumps `module = "ns:proto@1.0.0"` to `@2.0.0` without touching the schema or options. The run is reported as cached and the files generated by the old generator stay in use.

findings.summary: Changing an invocation's `output-dir` still counts as a cache hit, so nothing is generated in the new directory.
findings.detail: `cache_matches` hashes the output paths recorded in the lockfile, which point into the old directory, and never checks that they lie under `invocation.output_dir`. If the old files are still on disk, the invocation is treated as cached and the generator never runs. The new output directory stays empty, and the stale entry, still pointing at the old directory, is written back to the lockfile.

findings.summary: Stale-output cleanup deletes another invocation's freshly generated files when one output directory sits inside another.
findings.detail: `kept_by_dir` holds only the outputs of invocations whose `output_dir` is exactly that key. `reconcile_outputs` then walks each directory recursively and deletes every `#![generated]` file not in that list. If invocation A uses `gen` and invocation B uses `gen/b`, cleaning `gen` deletes all of B's outputs, which then forces B to re-run on every build.

findings.summary: A sandboxed generator can read any file on the host, because `read-file` paths go straight to `base_path.join(path)`.
findings.detail: `KilnHostState::read_file` passes the path supplied by the generator to `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, which just does `self.base_path.join(path)`. Absolute paths (e.g. `/home/u/.ssh/id_rsa`) replace the base path, and `..` segments are not rejected. An untrusted registry generator can therefore read arbitrary files and embed them in generated code, defeating the sandbox the module claims to provide. The reads are also non-deterministic and outside the project.

findings.summary: Failed generator reads are never recorded, so the cache does not notice when such a file later appears.
findings.detail: `read_file` records a read only when the load succeeds. A generator that probes an optional include, gets an error and falls back to other behaviour leaves no trace in `reads`. If that file is created later, `cache_matches` still reports a hit and the stale output is reused. In addition, the filesystem host maps every error to `IoError`, so the `NotFound` branch is unreachable and generators never see `host-error::not-found`.

findings.summary: Diagnostics from generators are relayed to the inner host only, so the CLI never prints them.
findings.detail: `run_generator` passes `self.inner.clone()`, the inner `wado_lsp` host, to `kiln_runtime::run_generator`. `relay_diagnostic` therefore calls the inner host's `emit_diagnostic`, which just stores the message and skips the CLI wrapper's stderr printing and log-level filtering. Errors and warnings reported through `host::emit-diagnostic` are silently dropped from the user's view.

grade.reason: No finding covers walk_and_delete propagating NotFound errors when files are removed concurrently. Finding 2 touches reconcile_outputs, but its point is deleting another invocation's files in nested output directories, which is a different root cause.

entries.defect: The op-only walker (gen_repeat_body) emitted every greedy/non-greedy Optional as a plain one-token first-set check, so it ignored the lowered strategy (lookahead, scan guard, shape lookahead, `??` ATN). Optionals inside LR-suffix bodies were therefore mis-decided.

findings.summary: When a speculative alternative fails, the cursor is rewound with `p.pos = saved` but the TreeBuilder is not rolled back, so the failed attempt's tokens and nodes stay in the CST.
findings.detail: In `gen_multi_alt_body_alt`'s Ambiguous fallback (partial-scan and no-scan arms, plus the plain save-and-rewind fallback), the generated code calls `_alt_N(p)`. If that returns `Err`, it does `p.pos = saved;` and tries the next alternative. Every `expect`/`match_*` and every rule wrapper now records events on `p.b`, but no `checkpoint()`/`truncate()` brackets the attempt (unlike `gen_rep_break_with_recovery`, which this PR does bracket). So any grammar that reaches this speculative path ends up with the failed alt's terminals and the successful alt's terminals both in the tree, plus an `Open`/`Close` pair from the rule wrapper. The result is a duplicated or garbled `CstNode` tree even though the parse reports success. The tree feeds `to_string_tree` and highlighting.

findings.summary: A required group with overlapping alternatives no longer fails when no alternative matches, so invalid input is accepted silently.
findings.detail: `gen_consume_group_store_op` (SimpleCst) and `gen_general_group_store_op` (General) used to end their overlap path with `if let None = opt { p.fail(...)? }`. That check is gone, and `gen_simplecst_overlap_loop` / `gen_general_overlap_loop` now take no arm and append nothing when nothing matches. These helpers are reached through `gen_op_inner_for_storable_repeat`, including the mandatory first iteration of a `+` repeat: both the scannable and non-scannable Plus paths skip the scan guard on the first iteration (`if !_plus_first { ... }`). So `(a b | a c)+` facing a token that starts no alternative now consumes nothing and succeeds without a diagnostic. The comment says the repeat guard already verified a match before entry, but that is false for the first Plus iteration.

findings.summary: On error, the left-recursive rule function leaves an `Open` node unclosed, so the caller's `finish_node` closes the wrong node and the partial tree is mis-nested.
findings.detail: `gen_lr_fn` emits `p.b.start_node(RK, _start); _atom(p)?; p.b.finish_node(...)`, and each suffix is `start_node_at(...); <ops with ?>; finish_node(...)`. The LR wrapper deliberately opens no node (`takes_min_prec`). So when the atom or a suffix element fails, the `?` returns with the LR node still open. The enclosing non-LR wrapper then runs `p.b.finish_node(p.last_end())`, which closes the LR node instead of its own, and every node above is shifted by one. This breaks the fail-soft promise that 'open nodes [are] folded by each wrapper's finish_node': the partial tree in a `ParseResult` with errors gets the wrong parent/child structure, which affects highlighting and tree consumers.

findings.summary: `to_string_subtree` searches for kind -1 when the rule name is unknown, and -1 is `K_ERROR`, so it can return an `<error>` region instead of an empty string.
findings.detail: The generated helper starts with `_kind = -1`; if no name in `GALE_RULE_NAMES` equals `rule` it still calls `result.root.find_child(_kind as NodeKind)`. `K_ERROR` is defined as `-1`, so if the root has an error-region child, an unknown or misspelled rule name renders that error subtree. The documented behaviour is to return "" when the rule is absent.

grade.reason: None of the findings addresses gen_repeat_body emitting Optionals as a plain first-set check that ignores the lowered strategy in LR-suffix bodies; they cover CST rollback, group failure, LR node closing, and to_string_subtree.

findings.summary: The save-and-rewind speculative alternative paths reset `p.pos` but not the `TreeBuilder`. On a successful parse, a failed alternative's tokens and nodes stay in the CST and are then appended a second time.
findings.detail: `gen_prediction_code_inner` (the Ambiguous branch with partial or missing scans, and the fallback branch) emits `let saved = p.pos; let r_i = _alt_i(p); if let Err(_) = r_i { p.pos = saved; }` and then tries the next alternative. The Parser methods now call `self.b.token(...)` and the rule wrappers call `start_node`/`finish_node`, so a partly matched alternative has already recorded events. Nothing undoes them: no `checkpoint()`/`truncate()` here, unlike the one this PR added to `gen_rep_break_with_recovery`. The parse can finish with no diagnostics, yet the returned `root` holds the tokens and subtrees of the abandoned alternative followed by the same tokens again from the alternative that won. Any start node left open by the failed alternative also shifts the nesting. This breaks `to_string_tree`, highlighting and any consumer of the tree whenever a rule needs this backtracking dispatch.

findings.summary: The post-loop `p.fail(...)` was removed from required overlapping SimpleCst/General groups, so when no alternative matches the parse continues silently instead of reporting an error.
findings.detail: `gen_consume_group_store_op` and `gen_general_group_store_op` used to emit `if let None = opt { p.fail(...)?; }` after the overlap loop. Now the overlap loop simply takes no branch when the lookahead is outside every group's first set. These functions are reached through `gen_op_storable_group_inner`, which runs as the body of `+` repeats. In `gen_op_repeat_star_plus_storable` the mandatory first iteration runs unconditionally (`while _plus_first || ...`; in the scannable path the scan guard is skipped while `_plus_first`). So `(A x | A y | B)+` followed by a token outside its first set now matches zero iterations and keeps going with no diagnostic. This is a missed diagnostic, and those inputs report `ok()`.

findings.summary: Node-kind constants are named by just uppercasing the rule name, so two rules that differ only in case produce duplicate `RK_` globals and the generated parser fails to compile.
findings.detail: `gen_node_kinds` (and `rule_kind_const` in parser_gen) emit `global RK_{NAME.to_upper}`. ANTLR4 parser rule names are case-sensitive, so a grammar with both `fooBar` and `foobar` (or `exprList` and `exprlist`) emits `RK_FOOBAR` twice. The typed emitter did not have this collision, because its type names keep the original casing.

findings.summary: `to_string_subtree` with a rule name that does not exist searches for kind -1, which is `K_ERROR`, so it can return an error-region subtree instead of an empty string.
findings.detail: `_kind` defaults to -1 when no entry in `GALE_RULE_NAMES` matches, and `find_child(_kind as NodeKind)` then matches any direct child whose kind is `K_ERROR` (-1). The documented contract is to return "" when the rule is absent, but on a tree with a recovery region it renders `(<error> ...)` instead.

grade.reason: None of the findings addresses the op-only walker emitting Optionals as plain first-set checks that ignore the lowered strategy. The findings cover CST rewind, a missing fail, constant name collisions, and the to_string_subtree lookup.

findings.summary: When a speculative multi-alt parse fails, the code rewinds `p.pos` but not the `TreeBuilder`, so tokens and nodes from the failed alternative stay in the tree.
findings.detail: The fallback dispatch in the multi-alt emitter (around lines 5692–5771: the 'partial scan: try parse' and 'save-and-rewind' patterns) emits `let r_i = _alt_i(p); if let Err(_) = r_i { p.pos = saved; }` and then tries the next alternative. Every Parser consuming method now appends to `p.b`. Each alt function, and every rule wrapper it calls, also pushes Open/Tok/Close events. None of these are discarded on the rewind: there is no `p.b.checkpoint()`/`p.b.truncate()` around the attempt, unlike `gen_rep_break_with_recovery`. Whenever an earlier alternative consumes some tokens before failing and a later one succeeds, the parse succeeds but the CST contains the same tokens twice plus orphan sub-nodes. That corrupts `to_string_tree`, highlighting, and any consumer of `result.root`.

findings.summary: A required group with overlapping alternatives no longer reports an error when no alternative matches, so invalid input parses as OK.
findings.detail: In `gen_consume_group_store_op` and `gen_general_group_store_op`, the overlap branch used to emit `if let None = {opt_var} { p.fail(...)?; }` after the overlap loop. The new code removed this check. `gen_simplecst_overlap_loop` and `gen_general_overlap_loop` now just take no arm when nothing matches. These store_op paths handle mandatory (non-Optional) groups, not only repeat bodies whose scan guard already checked a match. So a mandatory group like `(a b | a c)` silently matches nothing on input that fits neither alternative. Parsing continues with no diagnostic, and `result.ok()` can be true for invalid input.

findings.summary: On an error inside the LR atom or an LR suffix, the generated code returns through `?` without closing the node it opened, so the partial tree comes out mis-nested.
findings.detail: `gen_lr_fn` emits `p.b.start_node(RK, _start); _atom(p)?; p.b.finish_node(...)`. `emit_lr_branch_body` emits `p.b.start_node_at(_cp, ...)`, then the suffix ops (which use `?`), then `finish_node`. When the atom or a suffix element fails, the `?` returns before `finish_node`. The LR wrapper deliberately opens no node of its own for LR rules, so nothing closes it. The caller's later `finish_node` then closes the wrong (inner LR) node, and every enclosing node is shifted by one level. That breaks the PR's stated fail-soft guarantee that open nodes are folded as the error propagates. Non-LR rules avoid this because their wrapper uses `let r = call` without `?` and always calls `finish_node`.

findings.summary: `to_string_subtree` uses the sentinel -1 when the rule name is not found, which is the same value as `K_ERROR`, so it renders an error-region node instead of returning an empty string.
findings.detail: The generated `to_string_subtree` initialises `_kind` to -1 and only overwrites it when `GALE_RULE_NAMES` contains the requested name. It then calls `result.root.find_child(_kind as NodeKind)`. `K_ERROR` is also -1, so for an unknown rule name, if the root has an `<error>` region child, that region is rendered rather than returning "" as documented.

grade.reason: None of the findings address the op-only walker (gen_repeat_body) emitting Optionals as plain first-set checks while ignoring the lowered strategy (lookahead, scan guard, shape lookahead, or the `??` ATN).

entries.defect: For path-form method calls like `Scale::scaled(&p, 2, 3)`, the receiver is passed as `args[0]`, but self params were filtered from the parameter-name list, so every label shifted one argument left (`factor:` on `&p`, `bias:` on `2`).

findings.summary: `InlayHint` has no `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`, so the padding fields go out as `padding_left`/`padding_right` instead of `paddingLeft`/`paddingRight`.
findings.detail: The wire struct derives Serialize with snake_case field names. Every other LSP wire type in this crate (see `server/rpc.rs`) renames its fields to camelCase. LSP clients only recognise `paddingRight`, so they ignore the field. Every parameter hint then renders with no space before the argument (`a:1`), even though the code sets `padding_right: Some(true)` to stop exactly that. The unit test only checks the Rust field, and the wire test never looks at padding, so nothing catches it.

findings.summary: `record_local_symbol` keys the new `local_types` entries by `current_module_source`, but inherited trait default methods from another module are elaborated with that module's AstIds. Their parameter and local types land on unrelated bindings in the impl's module.
findings.detail: For a trait impl, the elaborator calls `resolve_method` on default methods that `find_trait_decl_methods` returns, and these can come from another module (for example core traits with default bodies). Their `param.id` and let-pattern ids are AstIds from the trait's module. AstIds are dense per module and start at 0, so `SymbolKey::new(self.current_module_source, def_id)` collides with real nodes in the implementing module. `local_types.insert` overwrites, so an inlay hint on a `let` or closure parameter in the entry module whose AstId matches can show the type of the foreign default method's `self`/`other`/local, e.g. `: &Point` on an integer binding.

findings.summary: A trait default method's body is elaborated once per implementing type, and `local_types` keeps whichever impl was elaborated last. Hints inside a default method body show one implementor's concrete types.
findings.detail: The trait declaration itself produces no TIR. Each `impl Trait for X` that does not override a default method re-runs `resolve_method` on the same AST, with `self` bound to `&X`. Each run calls `record_local_symbol` with the same SymbolKey and a different concrete TypeId, and the IndexMap insert overwrites the earlier one. So `let me = self;` or `let v = self.get();` in a default method body gets a hint naming the last implementor's types, which is wrong for the generic trait method the user is reading.

grade.reason: None of the findings address the self-param filtering in path-form static method calls that shifts parameter labels; they cover serde camelCase padding, cross-module AstId collisions, and default-method type overwrites.

findings.summary: Bindings whose type was never resolved get inlay hints that read `: unknown` or `: error`.
findings.detail: `push_type_hint` shows `local_type_name` without checking the type it gets back. That type is the `TypeId` stored by `record_local_symbol` when the local is added, and it is not always resolved. The clearest case is a closure parameter. `closure_param_type` returns `TypeTable::UNKNOWN` for an unannotated parameter when nothing gives it a type, as in `let g = |x| x + 1;`. `TypeTable::type_name` then turns that into the hint `: unknown` after `x`. In the same way, a `let` whose initializer has a type error is stored with the `Error` type and gets the hint `: error`. Both labels are wrong information shown inline in the editor. The PR's test `closure_param_without_annotation_emits_type_hint` does not catch this: it only checks that some type hint appears on line 1, and the hint for `g` already does that. Hints should be skipped when the resolved type is `Unknown` or `Error`.

grade.reason: The finding is about type hints that show unresolved `unknown`/`error` types. The known defect is about parameter-name labels shifting in path-form method calls, because self params were filtered out of the name list.

findings.summary: When a binding's type is still the `Unknown` or `Error` placeholder, the type hint shows `: unknown` or `: error` instead of being skipped.
findings.detail: `record_local_symbol` saves whatever `TypeId` exists when the binding is introduced. For an unannotated closure parameter with no expected function type (for example `let g = |x| x + 1;`), `closure_param_type` returns `TypeTable::UNKNOWN`. A destructured element that cannot be resolved falls back to `UNKNOWN` through `unwrap_or(TypeTable::UNKNOWN)` in stmt.rs. In code with type errors, bindings carry the `Error` type. `local_type_name` passes these straight to `TypeTable::type_name`, which renders them as "unknown" and "error", and `push_type_hint` never filters them out. The editor then shows a wrong `x: unknown` hint. The test `closure_param_without_annotation_emits_type_hint` only checks that some hint appears on the line, so it does not catch this.

grade.reason: The only finding concerns unknown/error type hints, not the shifted parameter-name labels caused by dropping the self param in path-form method calls.

entries.defect: The block parser let any list marker (e.g. a wrapped `2010) b` line), a link reference definition, or any HTML-tag-like line interrupt an open paragraph, and blockquotes had no lazy continuation, so the formatter rewrote paragraph text into lists, ref defs, or HTML blocks.

findings.summary: When a closure declares its return type (`-> T`), the missing-return and body/return type checks no longer run, so wrong closures compile without an error.
findings.detail: `return_type` becomes `declared_return` straight away when an annotation is present, which skips the `ast_find_return_type_in_block` / `ast_block_always_exits` MissingReturn check. Nothing compares the body type with the declared type either. As a result, `|x: i32| -> i32 { if x > 0 { return 1; } }` (falls off the end) and `|x: i32| -> i32 "s"` produce no error, and the compiler goes on to build an invalid or ill-typed function.

findings.summary: The formatter keeps only the first word of a fenced code block's info string and drops the rest.
findings.detail: `parse_fenced_code` stores only `first_word(info)` in `CodeBlock.tag`, and `print_code_block` prints only `cb.tag`. A fence such as ```` ```rust ignore ```` or ```` ```js {1,3} ```` is rewritten as ```` ```rust ```` / ```` ```js ````, so the annotations are lost when the file is written back.

findings.summary: Changing `*em*` to `_em_` ignores what comes before the opening `*`, so emphasis that follows a letter or digit is lost.
findings.detail: `keep_asterisk` is set only from `closer.next_is_alnum`. For `foo*bar* baz` the printer writes `foo_bar_ baz`. That `_` sits inside a word (both left- and right-flanking), so `can_open('_', ..)` fails and the reformatted text is no longer emphasis. The same happens for `a*(b)*c` → `a_(b)_c`.

findings.summary: Link and definition URLs written as `<...>` lose their angle brackets, so destinations that contain spaces stop being links.
findings.detail: `parse_dest_and_title` removes the `<`/`>` from the URL, and `print_dest_and_title` / `print_link_ref_def` print the bare URL. `[x](<a b.md>)` becomes `[x](a b.md)`, which re-parses with destination `a` and title-less garbage, or is not a link at all. Reference definitions with such URLs break the same way.

findings.summary: A nested list that follows a blank line inside a list item is cut out of the item and turned into a separate top-level list.
findings.detail:
In `parse_list`, a blank line continues the item only if the next line is not a list marker (`parse_list_marker(..) matches { None }`). So for `- a

  - b`, the item ends and `  - b` is parsed as a new top-level list. The formatter prints it as `- a

- b`, turning a nested item into a sibling. The printer can trigger this on its own output too: it forces a blank line after a Table/BlockQuote/Html child, so a nested list after one of those breaks out of the item when the file is re-parsed.

findings.summary: Any line starting with an HTML tag is treated as a raw HTML block, even in the middle of a paragraph, so formatting splits paragraphs and the renderer escapes the content.
findings.detail:
`is_html_block_start` is checked before text is added to the paragraph and accepts any tag, such as `` or ``. In CommonMark, type-7 HTML blocks must consist of the tag alone and cannot interrupt a paragraph. `text\nCtrl more` is therefore split into a Paragraph plus an Html block. The formatter inserts a blank line between them, changing the document structure. `render` outputs the whole block as escaped text with no `

` and no Markdown processing, and the block also swallows any following lines up to the next blank line.

findings.summary: `print_code_span` picks the wrong number of backticks and drops padding spaces, so some code spans change meaning when reformatted.
findings.detail: It uses "``" whenever the content contains any backtick, so content that itself contains a run of two backticks closes the span early. It also adds padding spaces only when the content starts or ends with a backtick. Content that originally had padding spaces, e.g. `` `  a  ` `` with content ` a `, is printed as `` ` a ` ``, and on re-parse one space pair is stripped again, leaving `a`.

findings.summary: Lists that differ only in bullet or delimiter are all printed with `-` or `.`, so separate lists merge on the next parse.
findings.detail:
The parser starts a new list when the marker changes (`- a
* b`, or `1.` vs `1)`). `print_list` always writes `-` or `N.`, and the two lists are separated by one blank line. The output `- a

- b` re-parses as a single loose list, which changes the structure (and the HTML), so formatting is not idempotent here.

grade.reason: Finding 5 says any HTML-tag-like line (type-7) interrupts an open paragraph and splits it into an Html block. That is one of the paragraph-interruption bugs the fix addresses by restricting interruption to types 1–6 and requiring a lone complete tag for type 7.

findings.summary: `render` panics on a link reference definition inside a list item.
findings.detail: `render_blocks` skips `LinkReferenceDef` and `FrontMatter` nodes. `render_item_child` does not: it sends every non-paragraph child to `render_block`, whose `_` arm panics. Inside an item, `parse_blocks` emits the definition as a node (`try_ref_def_line` matches the dedented line). So an input as small as `- [a]: /url` makes `render` panic with "unexpected node in block position".

findings.summary: A document that opens with a thematic break `---` and has another `---` later is read as YAML front matter, so the content between them is lost.
findings.detail:
`try_front_matter` accepts any first line equal to `---` and closes at the next line equal to `---`, wherever it is. Take `---

Intro

---

more`: the two thematic breaks and the paragraph between them become front matter. `render` drops front matter, so the paragraph silently disappears from the HTML; the old renderer produced `<hr />…<hr />`. `collect_ref_defs` also skips those lines.

findings.summary: Rewriting `*em*` to `_em_` drops the emphasis when an alphanumeric character comes before the opening delimiter.
findings.detail: `keep_asterisk` is set only when the character after the closing `*` is alphanumeric (`resolve_pair` uses `closer.next_is_alnum`). Nothing checks the character before the opener. For `foo*bar* baz` the printer writes `foo_bar_ baz`. An intraword `_` cannot open emphasis, so the formatted file renders the literal text `foo_bar_` and the emphasis is lost.

findings.summary: The printer emits link and definition destinations and titles raw, which corrupts URLs with spaces and titles with quotes.
findings.detail: `parse_dest_and_title` strips the `<…>` around a destination. `print_dest_and_title` and `print_link_ref_def` then print the URL bare and always wrap the title in `"`. So `[a](<x y>)` becomes `[a](x y)`, which reparses as URL `x` with the rest discarded. A title such as `'say "hi"'` becomes `"say "hi""`, which cuts the title short on reparse. The formatter rewrites files in place, so this loses data.

findings.summary: `print_code_span` always uses two backticks when the content has any backtick, which breaks spans whose content contains a run of two or more.
findings.detail: Code like ``` ```a``b``` ``` gives content `a``b`, which is printed as ``` ``a``b`` ```. On reparse the inner `` `` `` closes the span early and the rest becomes text. The fence width needs to be longer than the longest backtick run, as `fence_string` does for code blocks. Also, content with leading and trailing spaces (from `` `  a  ` ``) is printed with a single pad and loses its spaces on reparse.

findings.summary: The formatter turns trailing-two-space hard breaks into soft breaks.
findings.detail: The whitespace arm of `tokenize` drops spaces before a newline (`at_end`) and emits a plain `SoftBreak`. A GFM hard break written as `line  \n` is therefore printed as `line\nnext`, which changes how GitHub renders every file `marl-format` rewrites.

findings.summary: An explicit closure return type turns off the missing-return and body-type-mismatch checks.
findings.detail: When `declared_return` is present, `return_type` is set to it directly. This skips the `ast_find_return_type_in_block` / `ast_block_always_exits` MissingReturn check and never compares `body_type` with the annotation. So `|x: i32| -> i32 { }` and `|x: i32| -> i32 "s"` compile without a diagnostic. The closure's fn type then claims `i32` while the body produces unit or String, which can produce invalid Wasm instead of a type error.

findings.summary: Every bullet marker is normalised to `-` and blank-line separators are forced, so adjacent lists merge into one loose list.
findings.detail:
Lists with different markers (`- a\n* b`) or delimiters (`1. a\n1) b`) are parsed as separate lists. The printer gives both the same `-` or `N.` marker and puts a blank line between them (`prev_needs_boundary`). On reparse that is a single loose list, which changes the document's structure and its HTML (items gain `

`).

findings.summary: Image alt text keeps backslash escapes in the HTML output.
findings.detail: `text_to_html` resolves backslash escapes for Text nodes, but `render_image` passes `img.alt` (raw source) straight to `escape_attr`. `![a\*b](x.png)` therefore renders `alt="a\*b"` instead of `a*b`.

grade.reason: No finding addresses paragraph interruption by list markers, link ref defs, or HTML lines, nor the missing lazy continuation in blockquotes; the closest findings concern ref defs crashing the HTML renderer and front matter, which are different defects.

findings.summary: `render` panics when a link reference definition appears inside a list item.
findings.detail: `render_blocks` skips `LinkReferenceDef` nodes, but list items render their children through `render_item_children`, then `render_item_child`, then `render_block`. `render_block` has no `LinkReferenceDef` arm and reaches `_ => panic("marl-html: unexpected node in block position")`. `parse_blocks` emits a `LinkReferenceDef` node for any `[a]: /x` line, including one inside an item such as `- [a]: /x`. So rendering that ordinary Markdown traps instead of producing HTML.

findings.summary: A closure with an explicit `-> T` return type skips the missing-return and body-type checks.
findings.detail: When `declared_return` is set, `return_type` is simply `dt`, so the `ast_find_return_type_in_block`/`MissingReturn` analysis never runs. Nothing else compares `body_type` with the declared type either. `|x: i32| -> i32 { }` and `|x: i32| -> i32 { x; }` therefore compile without a diagnostic and are typed `fn(i32) -> i32`, while the body actually produces unit. A missing error then becomes ill-typed or invalid code further down the pipeline.

findings.summary: `strip_task_marker` treats `[x]`/`[ ]` as a task checkbox even when no whitespace follows, so a list item that starts with a link is corrupted.
findings.detail: The space after `]` is optional (`rest_start` only skips a space if one is present). An item like `- [x](https://example.com) docs` or `- [x]foo` is turned into a checked task with the rest `(https://example.com) docs`. `format` then prints `- [x] (https://example.com) docs`, which drops the link, and `render` shows a literal `[x] ` instead of an anchor. GFM requires whitespace after the checkbox.

findings.summary: Angle-bracketed link destinations are printed without their brackets, so a URL containing spaces is broken.
findings.detail: `parse_dest_and_title` removes the `<...>` around a destination. `print_dest_and_title` then writes the bare URL. `[a](<my file.md>)` becomes `[a](my file.md)`, which is not a valid CommonMark link. On reparse it yields url `my` and the rest is lost, so formatting silently changes the link target. The same applies to reference definitions printed by `print_link_ref_def`.

findings.summary: Titles are always re-emitted in double quotes without escaping, which breaks titles that contain `"`.
findings.detail: The parser accepts `'...'` and `(...)` titles, but `print_dest_and_title` and `print_link_ref_def` always print `"title"`. `[a](/u 'say "hi"')` is printed as `[a](/u "say "hi"")`. On reparse the title is cut at the first inner quote, so formatting loses data.

findings.summary: The keep-asterisk rule only looks at the character after the closing `*`, so emphasis opened inside a word is turned into `_..._` and stops being emphasis.
findings.detail: `keep_asterisk` is computed only from `closer.next_is_alnum`. For `foo*bar* baz` the opener is preceded by an alphanumeric character. Printed as `foo_bar_ baz`, the `_` opener is both-flanking with an alphanumeric before it, so it cannot open emphasis. The formatter silently removes the emphasis. The character before the opener also needs checking.

findings.summary: `print_code_span` uses at most two backticks, so a code span whose content contains a run of two or more backticks is printed wrongly.
findings.detail: `backtick_text` is "``" whenever the content has any backtick. Content such as ``a``b`` (from a span opened with three backticks) is printed between double backticks, and the inner `` closes the span early. Reparsing gives a different tree, so formatting changes the meaning. The fence must be longer than the longest backtick run in the content. Separately, content that begins and ends with a space is printed without the extra padding that would keep it intact.

findings.summary: Normalizing every list marker to `-` and every ordered delimiter to `.` merges lists that the source kept separate.
findings.detail:
The parser starts a new list when the bullet character or the ordered delimiter changes (`m.delim == base_delim`). The printer emits `-` or `N.` for all lists and separates them with a blank line. On reparse, `- a
* b` or `1. a

1) b` becomes a single loose list. So the output differs in structure from the input, and formatting the output again renumbers it, which also breaks idempotency.

grade.reason: None of the findings says that list markers, link reference definitions or HTML-tag lines wrongly interrupt an open paragraph, or that blockquotes lack lazy continuation; they cover other parser and printer bugs instead.
